Revealing the underlying visual concepts within a sketch is a crucial step towards reconstructing a 3D shape from it. Unlike literal sketch representations, concept-based sketches bypass unnecessary visual details for a more streamlined shape retrieval process. The aim of this research is to unlock the conceptual rendering of sketch ideas. We discover through user testing that programmatic searches through vast 3D shape repositories using conceptual sketches yield more accurate results compared to literal sketches. To tackle the inherent ambiguity in conceptual sketches, we introduce ShapeConcept, a comprehensive 3D shape retrieval benchmark centered on sketch concepts. We find traditional model-based approaches to 3D shape retrieval fall short in conceptual sketches, which we demonstrate through a thorough analysis. Instead, we develop and train a multi-modal shape concept embedding model that seamlessly integrates a ShapeNet dataset with written concept descriptions. The model's embedding accuracy surpasses existing 3D shape retrieval methods in conceptual sketches, marking a significant breakthrough in 3D shape conceptual retrieval. Additionally, our model's embeddings complement existing 3D shape retrieval methods, enabling these methods to focus on abstract shape concepts. Current theories in reinforcement learning posit that incorporating goals into training can significantly improve efficiency, particularly when working with intrinsic motivation, which learns objectives autonomously, or in conjunction with extrinsic rewards, which are dictated by human operators. However, it remains unclear how intrinsic motivation and extrinsic rewards interact, with most previous studies examining them in isolation or in simple scenarios. In contrast, we hypothesize that a purposeful, autonomous objective can augment a external reward signal, much like regularization objectives augment a human-defined reward. To test this interplay, we developed a novel, complex environment - the Grid World of Financial Trading - which enables autonomous objectives to augment an extrinsic reward. Our findings indicate that intrinsic objectives can enhance the efficiency of a training model by reducing variance when introduced early in training, particularly in scenarios where the target reward signal is suboptimal or poorly estimated. However, this is not the case when the reward signal is clear and the autonomous objectives are detrimental to the desired behavior, causing the model to converge to an alternative, unintended outcome. By providing a versatile environment for examining the interaction of intrinsic and extrinsic rewards, along with our corresponding findings, we contribute to an enhanced understanding of the role of objectives in reinforcement learning and the potential for intrinsic motivation to augment an extrinsic reward in more complex tasks. In this research, we focus on designing a multi-band 5G NR unlicensed/licensed system to address the issues of uncertainty in unlicensed band availability and varying licensed spectrum capacity. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel stochastic planning approach within a dynamic framework, enabling the simultaneous design of 5G NR unlicensed and licensed systems. Our approach incorporates the probability of unlicensed band being idle, along with the capacity of licensed spectrum, to optimize a multi-objective framework and yield a reliable and fair 5G NR system in both unlicensed and licensed spectrums. Our computational results demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed approach in enhancing the 5G NR unlicensed/licensed system, compared to individual optimization methods. Moreover, the advantage of using both unlicensed and licensed spectrums is evident, as well as the trade-off between our benchmark methods in terms of system reliability and fairness. Furthermore, the worst-case gap shows that improving the reliability-fairness trade-off in the 5G NR unlicensed/licensed system is achievable through the simultaneous design of both spectrums. To verify the practical applicability of our approach, we also considered the impact of frequency localization in the 5G NR unlicensed/licensed system and found that localizing frequencies below a certain threshold has a positive effect on system reliability and fairness. However, excessive localization may introduce a worst-case gap, highlighting the need for further research in this area. Finally, the illustrative examples and supplementary materials offer a deeper understanding of the 5G NR unlicensed/licensed system, as well as the stochastic planning approach and benchmark methods. The interaction between spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity has the potential to topologically transform the superconducting state, converting it from a second-order phase transition in a non-superconducting regime to a first-order phase transition within a superconducting regime. We investigate the phase transition between a non-superconducting $^3$He-A order parameter and a superconducting $^3$He-B order parameter within a narrow cylindrical channel placed in a $^3$He-filled dewar and cold fingers. The free fall along the dewar's cold finger may cause the $^3$He-A order parameter to undergo spin-orbit coupling-induced topological transformation before it is injected into the cylindrical channel. We demonstrate that the heat of transition and NMR spectrum change differ significantly in a superconducting regime compared to a non-superconducting regime. These findings can be used to determine the order of the phase transition and the nature of the superconducting order parameter within the cylindrical channel. We also discuss the feasibility of observing the Casimir effect on the heat of transition and NMR spectrum change in a superconducting regime compared to a non-superconducting regime. Our study shows that the Casimir effect may cause the phase transition to be observed at a lower temperature than predicted by thermal equilibrium conditions. We estimate that the Casimir effect may reduce the temperature by which the phase transition is observed by as much as 0.15 mk. Our study also shows that the Casimir effect may cause the phase transition to occur in a superconducting regime when it would otherwise occur in a non-superconducting regime, which may be relevant to upcoming $^3$He experiments in space. While some proponents of real theories claim that the phase uncertainty can be addressed through formal adjustments, we contend that doing so necessitates unacceptable alterations to the fundamental framework of QM. In order to validate our claims, we examine the foundational assumptions underlying real quantum theories and identify a common issue, namely that they all circumvent the principles that have come to be recognized as fundamental to QM. Furthermore, we offer a counterargument to the common assertion made by some researchers that the use of complex numbers is merely a matter of convenience or cultural influence. Instead, we propose that the utility of complex numbers is an inherent property of QM. In addition, we explore an alternative interpretation of the Aharonov-Bohm effect that highlights its potential to inform our understanding of the inherent role of complex numbers in QM. Finally, we outline the implications that the inherent use of complex numbers has for real quantum theories, suggesting that such theories introduce non-standard interpretations of the fundamental principles of QM. In particular, we consider real quantum theories as exemplifying a non-standard interpretation of the principle of superposition, in contrast to the more widely recognized form of the principle. In a corresponding discussion, we consider the implications of our analysis for other foundational challenges in QM, such as the nature of measurement and entanglement. In particular, we outline potential avenues for resolving measurement problems within the context of real quantum theories, while also acknowledging the inherent ambiguities that arise from non-standard interpretations of the principle of superposition. In addition, we present a measurement scheme in which the inherent use of complex numbers in QM is made explicit through the use of time-of-arrival variables that are informed by the principle of maximum entropy. Advancements in deep learning have enabled the creation of highly complex, black-box classifiers that are often difficult to understand and interpret. While these models can be easily trained and offer exceptional performance, their lack of transparency and accountability poses significant challenges. In particular, it is crucial to ensure that these models respect established social norms and operate in accordance with established ethical standards. One approach to addressing this limitation involves using symbolic surrogate models to facilitate a deeper understanding of the decision-making processes employed by black-box classifiers. By leveraging constraints induced by formal verification, it is possible to generate test data that can help to improve the transparency and accountability of black-box classifiers. In this study, we explore the development of symbolic surrogate models for image classification and present an approach for creating formal constraints that enable the creation of transparent and accountable deep learning models. Our proposed method involves using formal verification to produce test data that can help to refine the transparency and accountability of black-box classifiers. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method using the ImageNet dataset and a state-of-the-art black-box classifier, demonstrating that our approach can help to reduce the complexity and unpredictability of deep learning models while maintaining exceptional classification performance. Our results show that our method achieves accuracy and mean intersection over union (MIoU) scores of 82.78 and 65.13, respectively, with a 2.45 percentage point improvement in accuracy and a 3.99 percentage point improvement in MIoU scores compared to the baseline model. Furthermore, our approach offers a 14.90 percentage point improvement in MIoU scores with an additional 10.97 percentage point improvement in accuracy when compared to the baseline model, confirming the efficacy of our method in enhancing the transparency and accountability of deep learning models. In terms of computational efficiency, our approach requires 157.91 seconds to refine the decision-making process in the black-box classifier, with a significant reduction in computational cost. Our proposed method offers a 3.09 times faster refinement time compared to the baseline model, with a 3.09 times faster time to transparency and accountability. In particular, our approach can help to improve the transparency and accountability of deep learning models while scaling up to 1000 images. This study aims to shed light on these critical aspects by GCNs' over-smoothing problem, presenting an approach to mitigate the issue in the process. However, their effectiveness can be hampered by background noise and the irregularity of heart sounds that can lead to false positives. To address these limitations, we introduce a new method that utilizes a hidden Markov model to accurately identify and eliminate noise and irregular heart sounds. Our approach pre-trains a stacked autoencoder to create a rich, heart-rate-specific feature space that is then fed into a binary classifier to detect abnormalities. Our results demonstrate a significant 90% reduction in false positives on a widely-used clinical dataset, while maintaining a high overall accuracy of 94%. Furthermore, we utilize the Viterbi algorithm's probability values to calculate a confidence score for each detected heartbeat, which serves as a valuable metric for validating the correctness of automatic diagnoses. By minimizing errors and incorporating validation metrics, we can greatly enhance the performance and reliability of cardiac disease diagnosis using automatic heartbeat analysis. Our approach and associated code can be freely accessed on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/AUTOTimingBelt. Our code has been successfully tested on Windows 10 and Ubuntu 18.04 platforms. The standard single-particle perturbation theory is applied to determine electric dipole transition amplitudes across various isotopic variants of a given atomic symbol. The nuclear contribution to these transition amplitudes is calculated using the formula $\delta_a^{(n)}$, which measures the deviation in the nuclear wave function between isotopes. The total electric dipole transition amplitude for a transition between initial $i$ and final $f$ nuclear states, coupled with an electron, is calculated as the sum of the product of three factors: the nuclear contribution $\delta_a^{(n)}$, the core contribution $c_{if}$, and the tail contribution $t_{if}$, each applied to a different energy range of the atomic system. The core contribution accounts for the core-closed transition amplitudes within a defined energy range, calculated using the core properties of the atom. The tail contribution, which becomes significant for heavy atoms, is calculated using the finite nuclear mean volume $\overline{V}_a$ and weighted by the square of the electronic dipole transition amplitudes for a particular transition within that energy range. It's worth noting that the core and tail contributions ensure the validity of the nuclear perturbation theory for all isotopic variants of a given atomic symbol. Additionally, the total electric dipole transition amplitudes are correctly zero for certain'magic' isotopes with closed electronic shells, as well as for 'hollow' isotopes with fully occupied $d$-shells and a specific set of $s$-shell isotopes. The theoretical framework is then applied to calculate the nuclear perturbation-averaged electric dipole transition amplitudes for isotopes of Pb, Cd, and Ne. The results show that the tail contribution can become the dominant factor for certain heavy isotopes with low-core amplitudes, and that the derived transition amplitudes are in agreement with quantum mechanical expectations for light isotopes. However, the nuclear perturbation theory exhibits a notable deviation from the expected values for heavy isotopes, which is attributed to the insufficiency of single-particle perturbation theory in accounting for interactions between electron electrons. To validate the developed method, the calculated dipole transition rates and nuclear perturbation-averaged isotopic shifts for the $5p_{3/2}$ and $5p_{1/2}$ transitions in Pb are compared with the experimental values measured by Crawford et al. in 2010. The agreement between the calculated and measured values is found to be in excellent agreement for both sets

This research paper provides a detailed explanation of equivariant cohomology and some of its applications in topology. Specifically, we explore how using equivariant cohomology enables us to analyze and understand complex geometric and topological structures resulting from actions by finite groups on various manifolds. By delving into equivariant cohomology, we gain insights into characteristics like fixed points and homotopy equivalences in a topological framework. Furthermore, drawing from the principles of string theory, we examine the concept of twists, which arise from a circular action on a torus. Our analysis showcases the remarkable properties of twists as cyclic acyclic expansions of equivariant cohomology and reveals their intriguing connection with ringed topological structures. In addition, we investigate the properties of twists over tori and their correspondence with Hopf algebras. Finally, we apply these concepts to create twisted versions of ordinary cohomology, an approach with broad implications extending beyond the scope of this research. Some of the key findings of our study are demonstrated using the examples of $S^1$, $S^3$, and $S^1 \times S^1$. Our work is an adaptation of a previously published research paper by J. B. Fernandez and P. V. Kronheimer, although our approach diverges in several significant ways. Specifically, we make a distinction between a group action's twisted and twisted-influence aspects, unlike the authors of reference [6], who equate these concepts. Additionally, our formulation of twists contradicts the notion presented in reference [5], which is centered on orientable manifolds. Lastly, our analysis of the equivariant cohomology of $S^1$ and $S^3$ differs from the findings in reference [2], although our results align with their conclusions for $S^1$ and identify a previously overlooked generator in the case of $S^3$. Overall, the concepts of equivariant cohomology and twists offer a wealth of highly general and powerful ideas for studying a wide range of topological structures. The model was trained on a collection of 36,440 brushstrokes from 5 different style categories, including the brushstrokes of renowned artists David Hockney,or Sterrac, Frank Auerbach, Lucian Freud, and Joan Miro. The methodology employed a conditional GAN, with a stack of 3 convolutional layers in the discriminator and 2 transposed convolutional layers in the generator, and the model was found to produce impressive results that rival the quality of human-created art. The innovation represented by this model challenges the long-held view that human creativity is unique to humans. Instead, it suggests that the creative capabilities that were previously attributed to humans can, in fact, be captured by artificial intelligence. As a result, the model raises fundamental questions about the nature of art and creativity, and whether AI can be considered an artist. These questions are explored in depth within the paper, and in accompanying videos and online demonstrations. According to our simplified theoretical framework, the underlying reason for these fluctuations could be attributed to a particular type of right-handed current interaction that is not yet fully understood. This universal origin common to all these anomalies is a significant advantage, as it allows for the interpretation of the recent data from the LHCb experiment in the context of a combined flavor and lepton universality violation. Our analysis indicates that the combination of the violations of flavor and lepton universality provides highly competitive constraints on the parameters of the right-handed current interaction. This analysis is carried out within the context of a simplified effective field theory, using the resonance parameterization with the help of CaGlubRes library, which aids in extracting the resonance amplitudes. This analysis is done under the constraint of real right-handed current interaction and assumes the absence of double spin-parity contributions. As a result, the constraints on the product of coupling and coupling mass, which is related to the right-handed current interaction, is on the order of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-10}$, which is in line with the recent findings of the CHARM experiment. On the other hand, the universal contribution of the right-handed current interaction to flavor-violating $(V+A)$ amplitudes of neutral kaons and $B$-mesons is directly proportional to the difference in their couplings. Factors such as different methods for forming stellar iron cores and variations in the initial explosions influence these processes, which remain relatively understudied. Using three-dimensional simulations, researchers have been able to gain more insight into the role of material dispersal in the development and behavior of the post-shock region following a stellar explosion. Our studies have discovered that material dispersal plays a significant role in the creation and behavior of the material behind the shock wave. When a stellar explosion occurs in a dispersed environment, it results in the formation of large, extended structures behind the shock wave. These structures are characterized by complex and dynamic patterns, particularly in regions where the explosion occurs in a dispersed environment and the instabilities behind the shock wave amplify fluctuations in density and velocity, ultimately giving rise to fast instabilities. Conversely, when a stellar explosion occurs in a less dispersed environment, the post-shock region behind the shock wave exhibits relatively low amplitude fluctuations in density and velocity. Our simulations also highlight the significant impact that the formation of the stellar iron core has on the behavior of the explosion. When the core forms in a dispersed environment, it results in the creation of structures behind the shock wave that extend far into space. To mitigate this issue, a system was proposed to identify and distinguish between acronyms with unclear meanings. By developing a database of acronyms and their corresponding possible interpretations, the system was able to verify the correct meanings in specific domains and provide likely alternatives for unclear acronyms. Experimental results demonstrated the system's effectiveness in handling acronyms with multiple possible meanings and limited domain-specific acronyms. The main constraints of the current approach were primarily related to the quality of the annotated data and the complexity of the system's architecture, which compromised its efficiency. These limitations offer opportunities for further research and development to create more sophisticated and versatile acronym disambiguation systems. The benefits and drawbacks of the system, along with its potential applications and technical challenges, will be explored in potential future investigations. We propose a method of heat rectification using quantum Hall systems where a high-energy electron stream moves from a thermal source to a thermal sink, simultaneously propelling a corresponding flow of charge. This heat rectification mechanism can function even in systems that exhibit minimal charge conduction due to being in a non-equilibrium state. Notably, heat rectification can occur in systems that do not utilize electrical currents, instead relying on a temperature difference to drive a flow of particles. This concept is illustrated through simulation of rectifier devices consisting of multiple quantum Hall layers, showing the potential for significant thermal rectification ratios. Additionally, we outline a plan for experimental evaluation of this heat rectification phenomenon. Ultimately, the combined investigation of heat and charge transport in quantum Hall systems holds promise for advancing our understanding of mesoscopic physics and for generating novel thermal devices. \textit{See also \textit{arXiv:2101.01477} for an earlier version of this work.} \textit{All experimental implementation details have been added to the current submission following review.} Furthermore, the proposal involves calculating the thermal conductivity of quantum Hall insulators and the possibility of observing strong thermal rectification has been substantiated by numerical simulations. Recent advances in DNA sequencing technology have enabled the development of DNA-based data storage methods, allowing large amounts of data to be stored in extremely small volumes. The use of primers in DNA data storage, typically ranging from 24 to 114 base pairs, poses a challenge by limiting the size of information that can be retrieved from a single storage location, a problem exacerbated by existing primer designs. This work presents a novel storage technique that overcomes the 110-base pair barrier through a dual approach involving extended primers and specially designed storage partitions. The research offers a mathematical framework to optimize a prime number, essential for high-data-retention rates, and conducts experiments to demonstrate its practical applications. Although primary testing was conducted using a DNA microarray rather than a fully sequential storage system, simulation results indicate that the proposed technique can achieve nearly full data recovery with minimal errors. The research also validates the experimental protocol and provides guidance on how to effectively utilize a DNA pool to maximize data retrieval. Furthermore, the investigation explores the potential of the technique to support a robust yard-sign diameter of over 219 terabytes per storage unit, showcasing its vast storage capacity. The study's findings pave the way for an upcoming trial involving a fully sequential DNA-based data storage system, where the extended primer design will be put to the test. If successful, the approach has the potential to revolutionize the field, enabling the development of a fully functional DNA-based data storage system that can surpass conventional storage technologies. The research offers an innovative solution,primed for an upcoming opportunity to shape the future of DNA-based data storage. Topological nodal lines in momentum space are distinct from other topological states like Dirac and Weyl points, describing situations where the band structure intersects at a point rather than a plane, and this distinction is further highlighted by the presence of nodal lines in various materials. Despite their emerging interest, theoretical understanding and description of nodal lines remain somewhat fragmented, making it important to develop a unified description through the use of linear independent vectors representing the band structure's transformation under momentum changes. By representing the kinetic operator in a specific basis close to the nodal lines and performing a detailed analysis of its properties, the conditions necessary for the lines to exist are identified, and the potential phases of nodal lines in the studies of quantum systems are also discussed. Using this framework, the authors are able to explain and unify various concepts previously introduced to describe nodal lines, and their approach is further applied to illustrate key aspects of the lines' characteristics, such as their texture, anomaly, and fusion with Dirac points. The study is supported by the inclusion of experimental influences and the examination of common properties among materials containing nodal lines, enabling the authors to conclude by highlighting the potential for the studies to drive discoveries in the field, particularly through the use of computational and experimental methods to classify and navigate topological materials containing nodal lines. The authors also discuss the challenges and opportunities presented by the complex band structures of nodal line materials, and the potential for the study of these materials to drive new developments in condensed matter physics. The study is further supported by a comprehensive collection of additional resources, including illustrative examples, that delves deeper into key topics and themes. Using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, this model was found to match experiments precisely, providing a clear understanding of how these speeds are affected. This study also reveals that advanced mathematical concepts, such as nonlinearity and mode coupling, play a significant role in determining the best performing oscillator. By identifying the most effective attachment points and mechanisms for maximum wave speed, this model holds potential as an exclusive signal-generating system. Additionally, this study has far-reaching implications as it is similar to other physical systems, such as cells in biological tissues, (mechano)chemical reactions, and quantum systems. Therefore, this study has various applications across distinct fields of study. However, all oscillators produced similar wave speeds at certain high-frequency ranges regardless of the attachment point. Furthermore, these wave speeds were influenced by the mass and frequency of the oscillator. This paper investigates whether it's feasible to estimate the underlying probability distribution from observations of a marked point process, specifically the entropy of the process, given the constraint that a minimum amount of entropy must be present. We consider two scenarios: one in which a portion of the distribution, specified in advance, is known, and another in which no prior knowledge exists. In the first case, we find that under certain conditions, the entropy can be accurately estimated, under the constraint, using a method based on nearest neighbor labels. In the second scenario, we present an algorithm involving binarization and the shrinking of regions to determine the constrained entropy of the process. We verify that this algorithm is both efficient and reliable while also meeting the specified constraints. In support of the theoretical findings, we present simulations illustrating the functionality of the algorithms. In addition, the practical applications of the study are highlighted through its association with the analysis of traffic scenarios. We consider a partial distribution to be specified in advance as a priori knowledge and that the associated entropy as bounded as non-zero to be a constraining condition for entropy estimation algorithms, thereby facilitating their deployment in scenarios such as the study of network traffic, in which a partial distribution is known, while in the unconstrained scenario, we discovered an efficient and reliable algorithm for estimating the constrained entropy, thereby illustrating the practical use of the study through its association with the analysis of traffic scenarios. In particular, the prior work of Chan-Toumpas-Varadhan's result is extended in the entropy estimation, particularly on the instance where the partial distribution is known, while in the unconstrained scenario, the prior work of Bouman et al.'s result is refined in the context of marked point processes. Additionally, the total time complexity of the algorithm is found to be no greater than $\tilde{O}\left(M\left(\frac{N}{\log N}\right)^2\right)$, where $N$ is the number of points in the process and $M$ is the number of classes specified in the prior, thereby implying a nearly linear relationship when $M$ is small. Furthermore, the process of binarization and the reduction of regions is found to be efficient with a total time complexity of $\tilde{O}\left(N\log N\right)$. Lastly, the process of updating the region assignment is also efficient with a total time complexity of $\tilde{O}\left(\log^2 N\right)$. As deep learning continues to advance, there is a growing need for extensive, unstructured digital collections of medical images. Existing large-scale databases are often solitary, holistic collections of medical data. In contrast, the trend is shifting toward distributed, diverse image repositories. This work addresses the underlying challenges and opportunities for the creation and management of extensive, distributed medical image repositories known as imaging biobanks, with a focus on the specific requirements and issues these pose under the influence of artificial intelligence. Based on an in-depth analysis of current trends and the inherent complexities of imaging biobanks, we propose a comprehensive computational architecture and outline key implementation details. By examining the advantages and disadvantages of existing database systems in terms of their capacity, flexibility, and aptitude for handling complex data, we identify the most suitable systems for supporting complex data and implementing our proposed computational architecture. Specifically, we demonstrate that the MongoDB database system is particularly well-suited to providing a flexible, scalable solution. Ultimately, we provide a full implementation of our proposed architecture as an open-source solution known as MontImage DB. MontImage DB is currently available for free on the open-source platform GitHub, with full documentation and support also available through the MontImage DB community. The effectiveness of data augmentation in training machine learning models on medical notes depends on the presence of clinical features. If notes contain rich clinical information, the model will rely heavily on language patterns to make diagnoses, meaning any augmentation method attempting to modify words could compromise its performance. In contrast, when this clinical information is absent (e.g. in notes regarding COVID-19), data augmentation methods may face little opposition. As a result, simple, non-context-specific methods like word-replacement augmentation, which relies on pre-defined rules and doesn't need access to context, might actually provide a benefit in these situations. In this research, we tested this hypothesis, replacing medical notes with diagnoses from a particular category with different augmentation methods while keeping the original context. Our experiments compared four methods - word-replacement, word-swapping, sentence-replacement, and generation - using both natural language processing and machine learning models. Our findings show that the first method outperformed the others in predicting a specific COVID-19 diagnosis. In particular, when notes lack important context, method one performed better than the control model. Meanwhile, method two struggled in both contexts. Our evaluation also reveals that the benefits of data augmentation are sensitive to the clinical information available within the notes. In situations with limited context, simple augmentation methods can provide a solid foundation for model training. By combining this with the insights from model inspection, we found that the model's success with word-replacement likely results from its focus on pattern-based diagonalization. This research sheds light on the capabilities of data augmentation in medical settings with limited context. Our code is available on GitHub at this link. Polymatroidal ideals have distinct properties as their underlying rational normal cones possess complementary properties. Specifically, the rational normal cones have equitable dimension, and for any given point outside the cone, there exists a hyperplane that does not intersect the cone at that point. This characteristic translates to the associated linear spaces having suitable properties. This research validates the hypothesis that for any given polymatroidal ring, the collection of polynomials with lower degree than the ring's defining ideal forms a subring. This validation is accomplished by comparing the related \(\tau\)-spectrum and proving that one set is a subset of the other. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the subset relationship is generally not an equality, and provides criteria under which the subset relationship becomes an equivalence. As a result, the study yields various class inclusions of ideals, specifically in the context of monomial ideal ideals within polymatroidal rings. These findings imply the ring is subcoalgebraed by the collection of polynomials with lower degree than the ring's defining ideal, and as a consequence, the ring possesses certain algebro-geometric properties. These properties include, but are not limited to, the ring's projective variety being non-reducible and the variety's singularities being rational. The study also explores the relation of these properties with the properties of rational normal cones and complementary hyperplanes. The research delves into specific families of polymatroidal rings where the subset relationship becomes an equivalence, specifically the family of terminal polymatroidal rings and the family of hypersurface polymatroidal rings. In the case of terminal polymatroidal rings, the study shows the ring's defining ideal has a specific property and as a consequence, the ring is subcoalgebraed by the collection of polynomials with lower degree than the ring's defining ideal. Similarly, in the case of hypersurface polymatroidal rings, the study shows the ring's defining ideal has a specific property and as a consequence, the ring is subcoalgebraed by the collection of polynomials with lower degree than the ring's defining ideal. The study also initializes the study of specific families of polymatroidal rings where the subset relationship becomes an equivalence, specifically the family of sparse polymatroidal rings and the family of semi-stable polymatroidal rings. We introduce a quantum version of the K-means clustering algorithm, executed on a universal quantum computer utilizing a combination of quantum circuits and classical data processing. By leveraging quantum circuits, specifically the qubit state copying process, we develop a technique to efficiently handle high-dimensional data without excessive circuit depth. In experiments using a quantum circuit simulator and a quantum computer with 27 qubits, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Further research investigates the potential for combining multiple quantum algorithms into a single unified quantum clustering method. Both classical and quantum versions of the proposed algorithm were tested to establish a baseline for comparison. The extent of these events detects planets of very low mass relative to their host stars. We compiled a list of 271 planets discovered through transit in the Southern Hemisphere, covering a range of masses from $10^{-1}$ to $10^{-6}$ of the host star. We calculated the mass ratio of these planets and discovered that they fit within two distinct distributions, one for planets more massive than 10 times less massive than their host star and another for planets less massive than that threshold. The discovery of a peak in the mass ratio distribution at a value very close to 0.015, specifically 0.0137, is particularly notable. This peak is likely related to the formation of planets through the internal migration theory and may be verified by analyzing future discoveries of smaller planets. We found that planets with hosts that are part of multiple planetary systems are more likely to have lower mass ratios than those in single-host systems. This finding suggests that planets with low mass ratios may be more likely to be part of larger planetary systems in the future. Calculations based on the raw data of the Kepler mission also reveal that the detection of a particular type of planetary event, known as a multi-system small transiter, may be more likely for lower mass ratios. As a result, we may be missing detections of low-mass ratio planets within larger planetary systems in the Kepler mission data. Further research is necessary to confirm this potential issue. Ultimately, analyzing transiting planetary events could provide future discoveries of small planets with lower mass ratios that are currently undetected. This method employs a novel shadow map formation technique, utilizing the characteristics of photographic images to produce shadows quickly and efficiently, thus enabling fast and realistic shadow rendering for augmented reality applications. The obtained results show a substantial time savings of 2 to 3 orders of magnitude when generating entire uniform spanning forests of graphs with modest connectivity. The growing diversity in music representation methods is hindered by a lack of unified, large-scale music datasets, each tailored to address specific cross-modal retrieval challenges. To address this issue, the proposed MusicTM-Dataset is comprised of 8,786 million text-wheel pairs featuring diverse musical compositions and annotations, spanning multiple languages. This dataset is approximately 16 times larger than Music21 and 2 times larger than the MagnaTagATune collection, with its scale and complexity reflected in a massive text-wheel representation space of 446,440 dimensions. By incorporating parallel processing techniques, the construction of this dataset was accomplished in approximately 45 days using 80 machines. With its extensive size and complexity, the MusicTM-Dataset presents a demanding application for the development of cross-modal retrieval methods, offering a robust platform for the creation of more sophisticated music-related applications. At the time of writing, the dataset is available for download at a dedicated repository: https://github.com/yangyangyang1986/MusicTM-Dataset. Additionally, an open-source competition has been launched, inviting researchers to propose new methods for the handling of large music datasets: https://github.com/yangyangyang1986/MusicTM-Dataset-Competition. In this competition, the primary focus is on the exploration of new applications for the MusicTM-Dataset, with a comprehensive evaluation framework and 10 challenging tasks designed to stimulate innovative research in the field of cross-modal retrieval, music information retrieval, and related fields. With its potential to accelerate breakthroughs in these areas, we envision the MusicTM-Dataset to serve as a landmark reference for the community. The Lotse library is an open-source tool that provides a framework for implementing guidance strategies in cooperative robotics. Designed for collaborative robots, Lotse offers a versatile solution for developing and integrating a variety of guidance strategies, which are coded as independent modules. This framework's robustness is proven by its successful adoption in guiding the KHeRo robot at the University of Oldenburg and the BionicSpin robot at the University of Bremen, among other applications. This paper showcases the capabilities of Lotse through a software assessment, highlights its key benefits, and presents a modular control structure that enables the integration of guidance strategies. Additionally, the paper discusses ongoing and planned research related to Lotse, which focuses on expanding its functionality and exploring its potential in controlling physical interactions, moving beyond basic guidance to incorporate more complex behaviors, and incorporating learning capabilities into the library, ultimately aiming to explore the use of learning techniques in cooperative robotics, as illustrated by the recent integration of a learning module for the BionicSpin robot. Specifically, it shares connections with both the b-principle and stability theorems. By generalizing the MW-theorem through the use of spaces with frill boundaries, we are able to establish a new class of structures, which we have termed 'b-cycles.' Furthermore, the method employed in our theory allows for the consistent construction of all possible b-cycles, which in turn gives rise to a new invariant of the mapping class group. A balancing domain decomposition by constraints (BDDC) method is introduced for solving nonlinear elastic problems using the Kirchhoff plate equation. The corresponding algebraic system, derived from the finite element approximation, is then decomposed into sub-problems across the interfaces, and an analysis of their dimensions and structures is conducted. The convergence of the BDDC method is assessed in terms of iteration count, and its performance in relation to various parameters is investigated. Specifically, the influence of initial solution, flexibility parameters, and penalty values on iteration count is studied, as well as the effect of problem dimensions. Moreover, an optimization technique to determine these parameters is proposed and verified to be effective. The method's performance in terms of time and memory consumption is also evaluated, and an comparison with the Dirichlet boundary condition method is included. This study investigates how users label articles in news aggregator systems, where they assign tags to stories to create personalized feeds and discover new sources. Analyzing users' tagging behavior can inform the development of more effective content management features. We examined the tagging patterns of hundreds of users from Yahoo!'s 360° News, focusing on the tags they chose, how they used the system, and why they selected specific labels. Our findings reveal that users' tagging intentions often diverge from the system's predefined categories, leading to inconsistent labeling and reduced system effectiveness. These discrepancies create challenges for users and the system, particularly in determining the best category for a story and assigning labels uniformly. We believe that identifying such gaps between user needs and system functionality and developing targeted improvements can boost system usage and performance. Ultimately, these enhancements enable users to use the system more efficiently and effectively. Based on our findings, we suggest several system enhancements to address these challenges and make the news aggregator system more practical and useful. Yahoo! 360° News was used for data collection in Fall 2006, but the conclusions drawn from this study remain relevant to current tagging systems. The research was presented at CHI 2007. Subsequent validation using data from Flickr confirmed that the findings are generally applicable to other tagging systems as well. The overall goal of this research is to investigate how users label articles in news aggregator systems, understand their tagging behavior, and use these insights to develop improvements that can boost system usage and effectiveness. Such insights can be employed to design targeted system enhancements, which were proposed in the study. Recent experiments in acoustic metamaterials have highlighted the neglect of thermoviscous effects in their traditional designs using the classical Rayleigh dissipation model. To overcome this limitation, a new general model based on Navier's and Stokes' equations has been developed for microscale acoustic waves. This model incorporates the effects of thermoviscosity and random fluctuations in a heat conduction framework influenced by the non-equilibrium phonon-electron interaction. Various simplified models emerge from this fundamental equation by applying the heat conduction-asymptotic expansion method and representing the fluid's dynamic properties with power-law functions. By re-examining the dissipation model through an energy analysis, the physical origins of the observed dissipation behaviors are identified and the limitations of the conventional model are clarified. Furthermore, numerical simulations using the general model demonstrate that thermoviscous effects significantly influence the performance of specific types of acoustic metamaterials, potentially leading to unidirectional wave propagation and the creation of acoustic dark holes. To optimize these devices, accurate estimation of the thermoviscous hydrodynamic quantities is essential. This can be achieved by combining the general model with the Maximum Entropy Method, producing a thermodynamic model that accurately predicts microscale acoustic wave properties and behaviors. Experimental validation of the model is also conducted, demonstrating its efficacy in guiding the design of advanced acoustic metamaterials that utilize thermoviscous hydrodynamics to maximize their performance. Ultimately, the model's findings pave the way for the development of novel thermoviscous acoustic devices and technologies. Additionally, the model's applicability extends to the analysis of microscale thermal transduction and the optimization of thermal travel times in dark silicon photonic devices. This research not only delves into the thermoviscous effects on acoustic metamaterials but also explores the broader implications of thermoviscosity on cutting-edge micro/nano mechanical devices and their applications. By combining theoretical, numerical, and experimental approaches, this study sheds light on the complex thermoviscous behavior of acoustic waves at the microscale, enabling the optimal design of innovative thermal and acoustic devices. This research is expected to have a significant practical impact in the field of micro/nano mechanical systems technology. Furthermore, the general model proposed in this research may also be applicable to other types of waves in micro/nano pipes and other extreme conditions. By extending the scope of the model to elastic solids, the principles of thermoviscous hydrodynamics can be used to develop simplified models for various dissipation mechanisms and optimize microscale elastic wave devices.

Planck first proposed that the quantization of energy in the electromagnetic field occurs in discrete packets, or quanta, known as photons, to explain the discrete lines in the Balmer series. However, this approach faces a key challenge of reconciling continuous spectra in nature. To address this limitation, Bohr developed an uncertain quantum condition for energy levels, and later, Einstein introduced the concept of further constraints based on energy conservation. Ultimately, these efforts by Planck, Bohr, and Einstein led to the development of quantum mechanics through the contributions of numerous scientists. This article examines the significance and chronology of these key developments in the history of quantum mechanics. Unlike previous historical studies on the topic, this article delves into the specific contributions of Planck, Bohr, and Einstein, as well as the collective efforts of many other influential scientists. By exploring their personal relationships and interactions, this article sheds light on the intricate dynamics of the quantum community that facilitated the breakthroughs in the field. Additionally, this study proposes the concept of 'collective memory' to describe how the community's knowledge and discoveries evolve over time through processes of accumulation, transmission, and transformation. By applying this concept to the case study of quantum mechanics, this study demonstrates that the development of any groundbreaking idea often requires many years of collective efforts, where individual contributors play a crucial role in shaping the community's collective memory that ultimately gives rise to innovative advancements in the field. Finally, this study explores the relevance of the concept of 'collective memory' to the current global challenges posed by climate change, where the collective efforts of scientists and the broader community are required to address complex issues exceeding the lifespan of individual scientists. By analyzing the successes and failures of the quantum community, this study aims to illuminate the promising prospects for the community to address the pressing global issues of the 21st century. The vision for the future presented in this study posits a future where the community of scientists can utilize their collective expertise and knowledge to tackle the pressing environmental issues, where individual initiatives are interconnected and interdependent. By reflecting on the past and present contributions of scientists, this study reiterates the importance of recognizing the collective achievements of the quantum community, where individual discoveries are inextricably linked to the community's collective memory that gives rise to new paradigms in the field. The quantum community, characterized by its interconnectedness and interdependence, is shown to be a unique model for addressing the pressing global issues of the 21st century, where individual initiatives are integral to the community's collective expertise

By exploring different curriculum designs, which influence the transition between skill acquisition to skill refinement, we demonstrate their impact on converging to optimal solutions. Deep learning techniques have rapidly gained acceptance as information fusion strategies, with multiple approaches employed to integrate multiple sources of data. This study introduces a novel hierarchical fusion method that stands out from existing techniques such as early, intermediate, and late fusion methods by addressing the issue of balanced representation in the combined model. In contrast to early and intermediate fusion, hierarchical fusion learns a balanced representation by merging features from multiple sources at a higher level of abstraction, as opposed to combining them at a lower level of abstraction, like CNN features. This approach differs from late fusion, which merges models using a simple aggregation function. Additionally, the paper addresses the issue of overfitting using dropout and the likelihood method to estimate class probabilities. Experiments were conducted on the RFGPBA, RFGC, and SOTAs datasets to evaluate the performance of the hierarchical fusion technique. Notably, the proposed method achieved an accuracy of 68% on the RFGPBA dataset, outperforming other techniques including triple-task, double-task, and multi-task models by 13%, 10%, and 4% respectively, as well as early, intermediate, and late fusion methods on the RFGC dataset. Further analysis through the AUC-ROC curve confirmed the robustness of the hierarchical fusion method. This study's findings demonstrate that hierarchical fusion is a versatile technique, applicable to datasets with imbalanced classes, which has significant practical implications. The code for the hierarchical fusion method can be accessed at https://github.com/asharfi/hierarchical_fusion. In terms of generalizability, the study's performance on the SOTAs dataset surpassed that of other deep learning-based information fusion techniques. Specifically, the hierarchical fusion method outperformed the triple-task, double-task, and multi-task models by 8%, 6%, and 4%, respectively, as well as early, intermediate, and late fusion methods on the SOTAs dataset. Additionally, the study's performance using the likelihood method exceeded that of the baseline triple-task model on the RFGPBA dataset by 4%. Furthermore, the study's performance using the likelihood method exceeded that of the baseline double-task model on the RFGC dataset by 3%. Overall, the hierarchical fusion method represents a highly effective information fusion technique, adaptable to imbalanced classes. The COVID-19 pandemic has put a tremendous strain on medical systems around the world, highlighting the importance of efficiently allocating limited intensive care unit resources. To combat the crisis, doctors and researchers are seeking effective ways to predict which patients are at higher risk of needing critical care so that ICU resources can be allocated more equitably. Many of these methods, however, rely on complex and difficult-to-interpret models. In this study, we explored a different approach, focusing on detecting the distinct operational characteristics of patients who were admitted to the ICU. By analyzing a large combined dataset from multiple hospitals, we identified a set of distinct features related to ICU admission that are consistent and meaningful. We then developed a simple and intuitive method to detect patients at high risk based on these features. This study examines the transmission eigenvalue problem in a comprehensive study. It centers on a medium-defined ball in a higher-dimensional space, $ \mathbb{R}^{N} $, surrounded by a limitless, homogeneous medium. Researchers have long known that the transmission eigenfunctions localize perfectly around the boundary of a $ \mathbb{S}^{N-1} $ sphere in constant-medium scenarios. This paper confirms that those transmission eigenfunctions localize perfectly around the $ \mathbb{S}^{N-1} $ sphere in a medium-defined ball scenario as well. Additionally, the paper's results demonstrate the localization of these eigenfunctions to be absolute, depending solely on the medium parameters, $ \eta $ and $ \beta $, which are constant. Based on this discovery, the paper presents conditions under which the transmission eigenfunctions localize around the boundary of the ball, $ \mathbb{B}^{N} $, in a constant-medium scenario. Ultimately, the paper's results provide insights into the transmission eigenfunctions' behavior within the medium-defined ball and constant-medium scenarios. The research methodology utilized is quite unique, relying on the use of first-order PDEs and semilinear problems to derive the desired solutions. Additionally, the paper provides order-of-magnitude estimates and energy analyses which, although straightforward, contribute significantly to the understanding of the transmission eigenfunctions' behavior. To confirm the theoretical findings, the research presents numerical results and associated localization experiments. Finally, the research concludes with a set of open challenges and areas for further investigation. This research contributes to the existing literature on the transmission eigenvalue problem, particularly in scenarios involving media with variable properties. The research has far-reaching implications, extending to various fields including the study of seismic waves and the behavior of sound waves in different media. Our experiments examine the effectiveness of different pre-training objectives and vocabularies, as well as reduced-vocabulary strategies. Additionally, the model's ability to capture multi-modal representations, including semantics, syntax, and articulation, has been found to significantly boost its overall performance. Furthermore, the advantages of adaptation and the benefits of multi-task learning have been confirmed through ablation studies. The framework of JASPER will serve as a basis for further optimization and research in representation learning for speech. With its enhanced capabilities and reduced vocabularies, the model will be applied in tasks such as speech recognition and audio visual translation. The paper addresses the issue of finding a suitable gauge transformation to reduce the Sitter kappa-deformed higher-spin equations to their non-deformed forms. A particular gauge transformation, analogous to the BRS transformation but using the $S^{(1,0)}$ operator, has been found and shown to converge to the Zinoviev gauge for $S^{(2,0)}$. Furthermore, it has been found that the continuum limit of the $S^{(1,0)}$ variable is closely related to the Korteweg-de Vries equation, specifically in the Fokas transform form. These findings imply that the gauge theory itself can be interpreted as a quantum field theory describing the interaction of soliton-like objects with the Korteweg-de Vries wave field. The paper discusses the implications of these results for the broader "deformation technique" and their potential applications in mathematical physics. Additionally, it outlines a systematic approach to finding suitable gauge transformations of a specified form for any given Sitter kappa-deformed higher-spin equation. The approach involves adapting the relevant form of the antibracket operator to the deformation parameters of the equation, thereby summarizing the process as the ABRE formulation. The ABRE has been found to encompass the Sitter deformation of the massive free higher-spin fields within the de Sitter space context. The results of the work may be of interest in the context of quark-gluon plasma physics, as the conventional Yang-Mills theory used in this area is seen to emerge naturally from the general form of the ABRE when the deformation parameters are set to zero. When the deformation parameters are non-zero, the ABRE describes the interaction of Yang-Mills fields with a nonlinear scalar field derived from the Korteweg-de Vries equation, thereby describing a more complex system than typical Yang-Mills theory used in this area. The paper, therefore, suggests alternative approaches to describing the quark-gluon plasma, specifically by its interaction with soliton-like objects and their consequences for particle multiplicity measurements. Finally, the potential of the deformed equation for describing real-world particle multiplicity in quark-gluon plasma may be explored using the relevant experimental data available from the LHC. Visual Relationship Detection (VRD), a critical problem in computer vision and natural language processing, is involved in identifying multiple attributes (e.g. object-object, color-color) within an image. Current deep learning approaches to VRD have achieved impressive results, albeit at a costly expense: they require substantial amounts of data and advanced computational power. To tackle the challenging issue of data scarcity, the optimization technique must be refined. A proposed strategy, Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), attacks this problem by sampling unselected options in a more balanced manner to minimize biased model predictions. The results show that BNPS outperforms conventional techniques in VRD tasks, specifically on the Visual Relationship Detection task in the MVTec AD dataset and the Visual Relationship Detection challenge in the COCO-Stuff-10K dataset. Notably, the efficacy of BNPS was verified across various deep learning models, including those based on a two-stage framework and others involving a single-stage design. The advantages of BNPS are best exemplified in scenarios involving limited data; in such situations, the approach consistently surpasses alternative techniques by at least 2%. A further investigation into the mechanisms driving BNPS revealed that it prompts the model to explore a wider range of unselected options, thus minimizing biased predictions. The findings also indicate that BNPS's effectiveness is sensitive to data availability: with ample data, the benefits of BNPS diminish, and it no longer outperforms the conventional technique. In computer vision, Geometric Gated GANs were introduced to address issues with unconditional non-identical transformations in object reconstruction. Their concept, Gated GANs, was shown to improve generalization. Building upon this, we propose the Relationship Gated GANs, combining it with graph neural networks to learn relationship states and dynamics in social interactions, ultimately generating realistic scene responses. By incorporating Gated Recurrent Units within a graph neural network, our model learns to update relationship states with temporal context. By integrating Gated GANs, we capture diverse, directional social links within a scene, such as colleague, family, or friend relationships. By learning these relationships, our model generates more realistic, varied social interactions, ultimately enhancing scene responses. We demonstrate the efficacy of our model through qualitative analysis of generated interactions and a comparison of its performance on a social interaction dataset with a baseline method. Our model, GAN-Relationship, is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharakeh/Relationship-GAN. Experimental results indicate that GAN-Relationship surpasses the baseline method in generating realistic social interactions, with an increase of at least 5% in Inception Score and at most 10% in variation of occurrence for different family structures in the FamilyRoom dataset. Specifically, GAN-Relationship achieves an Inception Score of 2.07 and 2.28 on FamilyRoom and SocialMedia datasets, respectively, an increase of 5% over the baseline method. Moreover, the generated social interactions in FamilyRoom and SocialMedia are now 10% more diverse, as gauged by Variation of Occurrence, over the baseline method. Previous approaches assume that the error propagation rule is perfect, but in reality, this rule is not perfect and can omit certain errors while introducing new ones. By taking into account the actual error propagation rule, researchers have developed a method to accurately quantify the amount of memory needed for a given error rate, resulting in better estimates compared to previous approaches. Furthermore, this method allows for the determination of whether a given error rate can be achieved and how many error-values are necessary. We provide closed-form formulas for popular error propagation rules and an algorithm is also proposed to optimize memory usage based on the error rate and another metric, called circuit height. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to several benchmarks and finding that circuit area can be reduced by up to 15% or the height of circuits can be reduced by up to 40% depending on the error rate. Consider the set $\mathcal{S}$ of natural numbers that can be expressed as the sum of squares and additive complements, where the former has coefficients of 1 and the latter has coefficients of 0 or 1, respectively. Fourier analysis methods have been successfully applied to investigate the asymptotic behavior of the set $\mathcal{S}$ and its associations with other number theoretic problems in the past. We are now presenting an improved asymptotic estimate for the count of $\mathcal{S}$ numbers, addressing a previous challenge posed by Choi and Huang, with our result showcasing a substantial improvement over the conventional estimate of $x^{1/4}$. To achieve this breakthrough, we capitalized on a novel property allowing the direct utilization of the prime number theorem on the set $\mathcal{S}$ numbers. Moreover, we also derive the prime count within the set $\mathcal{S}$, which is defined as $\mathcal{S}(x)$, where $x$ is a natural number. By leveraging this prime count, we are able to compute the asymptotic probability of a sum of squares and additive complements being a prime, leading to the derivation of the prime count within the set $\mathcal{S}$ again. Lastly, our research enables the asymptotic estimation of the count of $\mathcal{S}$ numbers, where the boundary is defined by the function $\psi(x,\Lambda)$, which represents the Chebyshev's function extended to the set $\mathcal{S}$ numbers. Data augmentation through random transformations (e.g. rotation, flipping) is a well-known technique for boosting Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) performance. By producing diverse input data, this method enhances the diversity of the network's predictions, effectively reducing overfitting. In this study, a novel data augmentation approach using super pixel delimiting masks on images is proposed. By manipulating these masks, diverse data augmentations can be achieved with minimal computational effort, facilitating efficient use of GPU resources. A comprehensive empirical study examines the efficacy of this technique across different network architectures, hardening devices, and applications (human action recognition and road sign classification), with results indicating its effectiveness in enhancing model robustness and performance. Furthermore, the advantages of this method over existing techniques, such as cutout, cutpaste, and mixup, are discussed in depth. Additionally, a open-source code base has been established on GitHub to empower reproducibility and ongoing research. Our findings demonstrate that combining this new data augmentation method with existing techniques (random erosion and mixup) yields superior performance, underscoring its value as a useful tool in computer vision. Specifically, the best performance was achieved when each method was applied independently, resulting in a 1.38% error reduction over a baseline model trained with standard images. Moreover, the efficacy of this approach in safeguarding model robustness was confirmed through experiments on both hardening devices and perturbation methods (e.g. image cropping, filter substitution). Notably, the benefits of this technique were most pronounced for network architectures with pre-trained features, underscoring its potential as a pivotal tool in the computer vision community. With a validated cod base and accompanying data, we hope to inspire further research into the effective data augmentation methods in deep learning for computer vision applications. Through the reproduction of our results, we aim to promote the development of novel data augmentation techniques that can enhance model performance and robustness in diverse network architectures, applications, and hardening devices. A comprehensive code base has been established on GitHub to support the reproduction of our studies on human action recognition and road sign classification. Moreover, the open-source repository includes the necessary code for the development of the OpenCV-based data augmentation tool, as well as the creation of delimiting masks at different sizes, which can be found in the `augmentation_utils` folder. Using citation analysis, our work examines the research priorities of climate change researchers from 1995 to 2020 in relation to those of economists and general science researchers. Interestingly, a distinct pattern emerges where the interest of policymakers in climate change is actually lower than the general interest or expertise. This finding is further supported by qualitative evidence showing that a significant proportion of climate change research is not directly focused on the most critical issues from a policy perspective. Furthermore, our analysis highlights a notable lack of investment in the fundamental research necessary to address the most pressing climate challenges as identified by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. To better understand the priorities of climate change research and effectively utilize scientific knowledge, we suggest enhancing research evaluation methods by incorporating more diverse stakeholders and their corresponding research priorities. Ultimately, our research aims to promote policy-relevant climate change research by illustrating the disconnect between current research priorities and those necessary to combat the most severe climate issues. We present two key results that contribute to the irreducibility of tensor products, specifically involving highest weight modules and U(𝕙)-free modules, within the universal enveloping algebra of a semisimple Lie algebra. Firstly, we establish that irreducibility can be determined by examining the isomorphism to a specific module, U(𝕙)v_, where v_ is a non-zero vector whose orbit under the action of U(𝕙) generates the entire algebra. Secondly, we prove that tensor products of highest weight modules and U(𝕙)-free modules are irreducible if and only if a certain condition is met, specifically involving the intersection of two subalgeers, U(𝕙)v_ and U(𝕙)w_, for any non-zero vectors v_ and w_ whose orbits under the action of U(𝕙) are distinct. The role of role specifications in role-playing dialogue contexts involves
representing the roles taken by participants in a conversation. This role
category encompasses various personality types and functions, such as listener
and speaker. Role specifications in dialogue systems can significantly impact
performance, given that a dialogue model's ability to engage in natural and
coherent conversations is largely influenced by its understanding of the
roles involved. Current dialogue models, despite being trained on role-playing
data, frequently fail to recognize role-specific tasks and requirements.
Notably, existing research on role specifications has focused on using external
memories to store role information and guide dialogue responses, rather than
incorporating role specifications into the dialogue model itself. This model,
called the Role Specification Model (RSM), uses role specifications to inform
dialogue responses through role-aware representations and a common set of
general knowledge. RSM's representations comprise role-aware elements,
combining role information with contextual data, while its objective includes
minimizing divergence from role-specific goals. RSM's training involves
optimizing performance based on both role-specific goals and overall
conversational effectiveness. Experimental evaluations demonstrate RSM's
ability to achieve role-specific tasks and requirements while maintaining
coherent and natural conversation. Additionally, RSM's performance compares
favorably to state-of-the-art systems. Further analysis into RSM's
representations and its role specifications reveals that RSM's role-aware
elements are highly similar to role-specific goals and requirements. Also,
also, RSM's ability to engage in natural and coherent conversations is
greatly influenced by its role specifications. This research challenges the
notion that role specifications must be stored in external memories to guide
dialogue responses and instead proposes a more effective model, the Role

This method has been found to produce a 10 times faster mesh generation compared to traditional mesh generators. The resulting mesh has been accurately partitioned into evenly sized cells across 8 processes, leading to a considerable increase in performance of up to 15 times over certain kernels. This paper investigates the properties of vehicular networks comprising a mixture of ground stations, mobile stations, and relays to determine their capacity under conditions of interference, distance, speed, and road layout variability. We develop an analytical framework for a heterogeneous network featuring multiple ground stations, relay stations, and vehicular users to investigate capacity under interference and distance. Additionally, we investigate the impact of speed on capacity using an effective rate metric that indicates a decrease in capacity with increasing speed. We compare the capacity of networks featuring fixed and moving ground stations and find that the effect of speed is more significant in networks lacking ground stations. We also develop an effective rate model for networks with ground stations and a large number of relay stations and users, and propose a simple deployment strategy for ground stations and relays to maximize system efficiency. Our numerical findings demonstrate the accuracy of our analytical models and reveal the considerable influence of speed. We also identify a trade-off between the effects of distance and speed on capacity, and observe that the ideal ground station density depends on the network's speed variability. Our results are most relevant to urban areas with high speed variability. To validate our findings, we conduct simulations under conditions of speed variability and observe results consistent with our analytical models. Finally, we outline practical implications of our findings for vehicular network design. Our work is relevant to ongoing standardization efforts in 5G New Radio for vehicular applications. Ground stations may be deployed along main road arteries and at intersections to maximize coverage and speed support. Additionally, ground stations and relays should be positioned close to each other but far from incoming signal paths to optimize performance. Our findings also suggest the need for more rigorous outdoor channel modeling to accurately determine the effect of distance on capacity. Due to the difficulty of acquiring expert knowledge in certain areas, current learning methods rely on extensive, often artificially created, expert demonstrations to improve performance. However, creating and labeling data is labor-intensive; it's nearly as costly as hiring actual experts. We propose a novel concept, called Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), where multiple learners with different expertise exchange their knowledge and learn from each other. In a series of experiments with various tasks - ranging from simple classification to complex reward maximization in Atari games - CoIL consistently outperformed traditional imitation learning methods that relied on artificial expert demonstrations. Furthermore, CoIL's performance compared favorably to that of independently trained experts with unique problem-solving approaches. Our research demonstrates that collaborative learning among experts with diverse insights leads to improved performance and shows great potential for applications in a variety of domains. The unique two-handed interaction pattern of humans poses significant challenges for tracking systems. Specifically, hand object interactions that involve frequent occlusions of important objects or hands require sophisticated tracking techniques to maintain accurate object and hand localizations. Current top-performing tracking algorithms, designed for unobstructed views, are ineffective in addressing the complexities of occluded cases. Our solution, AOTrack, is an Occlusion-Aware Multi-Object Tracking algorithm specifically tailored for hand object interaction scenarios. By integrating specific features into a conventional differentiable tracking framework, AOTrack captures the patterns of object occlusion and easily shares information with other objects within the scene. Through extensive testing on complex hand object interaction datasets, our approach demonstrates superior tracking accuracy and a notable improvement in frame rates compared to the state-of-the-art method, with only a marginal increase in computational efficiency. Recent advancements in deep learning significantly affect visual-based human-machine interaction by increasing the complexity of required calculations. Nevertheless, the output precision of conventional end-effector pose estimation techniques severely suffers from the absence of adequate depth information, necessitating intricate and time-consuming spatial calibration processes which are largely dependent on visible light. When confronted with low-light or opaque working environments, these calibration processes become utterly impractical. In order to address this limitation, this research proposes the use of a depth camera to enhance the robustness of self-calibration methods for precise end-effector pose estimation in complex environments, particularly in low-light conditions. First, a new hand design template is created with implicit explicit corresponding features to enhance pose estimation performance. Secondly, a depth-based implicit representation learning approach is developed to leverage depth information for end-effector pose estimation. Thirdly, a refinement GAN is designed to recursively improve the precision of estimated poses in an iterative process. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing approaches in both explicit and implicit representation scenarios. Specifically, it achieves remarkable gains of 41% and 34% over the leading techniques in terms of precision when working in the dark and with occlusions, respectively. Moreover, the framework's robustness in space is validated through extensive experiments, demonstrating an impressive stability of pose estimation with minimal variance of 0.63 cm over a vast range of depths even in the absence of visible light.
