The building blocks for creating an extraterrestrial construction and manufacturing infrastructure are the local materials and their properties. Researchers from DLR and Kyoto University investigated the mechanical characteristics of Martian and Lunar soil or regolith by developing advanced testing equipment using 3D printing technology. The aim is to establish a unified testing standard for assessing the mechanical properties of extraterrestrial materials. Several samples from various sites on the Moon and a simulated Martian environment were tested using dynamic and static loading methods. The findings include the viscoelastic properties of Lunar regolith and the coexistence of water content and plastic deformation in Martian regolith. The study's outcomes can be utilized in designing infrastructure on other planets and in extraterrestrial manufacturing. The innovative testing equipment also contributes to advancing printing technologies for planar materials and structures. The collaboration between DLR and Kyoto University will lead to more groundbreaking research in constructing and manufacturing facilities on other planets. The partnership will also foster advanced technological development in space exploration. The study's results can be found in a forthcoming article in Acta Astronautica. The project received funding from DLR through the GLAM program and from JAXA, whose details are also mentioned in the study. The team from Kyoto University conducted the experiments at DLR's Institute of Space Systems in Bremen, Germany, under the supervision of Prof. Takashi Yoshizawa. The study's results are as follows: The compressive strength of Lunar regolith ranged from approximately 0.25 to 4 MPa, displaying viscoelastic characteristics under dynamic loading, with shear stresses reaching up to 0.22 MPa. The samples from Martian Site 1 exhibited plastic deformation and water content, with viscoelastic properties and a maximum shear stress of 0.32 MPa. The testing equipment successfully demonstrated its effectiveness in assessing the mechanical properties of regolith under varied loading methods, achieving reproducible results for each site. The study concludes by highlighting the potential for applying the test data in designing infrastructure, including buildings and manufacturing structures on other planets, as well as in developing new printing technologies for planar materials and structures. The outcomes can also be utilized in assessing the feasibility of using local materials for constructing life-supporting structures on other planets. The study's results can be expanded to include additional samples from other sites on the Moon and from Mars. The project's next steps will involve leveraging the test data in designing infrastructure, manufacturing structures on other planets, and in developing innovative printing technologies for planar materials and structures. The collaboration between DLR and Kyoto University will continue

This leads to the discovery of a previously unknown connection between certain groups within orbifolds and a specific subset of 2-step nilpotent groups, known as the Golod-Shafarevich groups. Golod-Shafarevich groups emerge as the key ingredient in developing a significant criterion for detecting potential rational Chern classes of orbifolds, with far-reaching implications for characterizing orbifolds with rational Chern classes. Utilizing this algorithm, we successfully classify and present a complete list of orbifolds with rational Chern classes up to a specific point of complexity, encompassing a broad range of categories, including symplectic and Gorter-Lindenberg quadratic categories. Lastly, our research highlights an intriguing dichotomy in the characteristics of orbifolds with rational Chern classes and their corresponding dual categories, highlighting a pressing need for further investigation into the relationship between these categories and the nature of their underlying orbifolds. We were asked to create an application that recognizes individuals sitting or standing in the living room and determines whether they are engaged in a device-based activity or not. As the largest and most complex biometric dataset, FaceNet poses significant challenges for cross-domain generalization in vision tasks. Traditional approaches using domain generalization or adversarial training are insufficient for unlocking the full potential of FaceNet. To address this gap, we propose a zero-shot framework that allows for seamless and unseen-data-extensive knowledge sharing across domains in a federated learning setting. By integrating meta-learning and adversarial training, our framework decouples class weights from loss functions, enabling the former to adaptably determine task-dependent losses while the latter enables cross-domain model sharing. Through iterative adversarial training, our framework empowers a single model to generalize across multiple domains on FaceNet, outperforming state-of-the-art domain generalization methods and adversarial approaches while also demonstrating zero-shot generalization across domains with unseen data distributions. This research presents an optimization-based joint channel estimation technique that leverages IEEE 754-2008 standard-compliant quantization of channel impulse responses at IRS-assisted systems. By treating the unitary components of the IRS phase shifts as optimization variables, this method directly estimates the cascaded channel coefficients, thereby yielding improved accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be viewed as a part of an optimization problem with an equality constraint set, which can be solved efficiently using unconstrained optimization frameworks like the generalized augmented Lagrange method. Simulation results reveal that the proposed solution outperforms existing benchmark methods, with superior performance in terms of least squares error and minimal decrease in uplink power over various channel conditions. Moreover, the optimal solution can be approximated with high precision when the number of IRS elements exceeds 48. In addition, the optimal quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) schemes and closed-form expressions for maximal ratio combining (MRC) and maximum likelihood (ML) decoding are also provided. During the coronavirus pandemic, local media played a crucial role in informing the public. However, the emphasis on COVID-19 coverage varied significantly across regions, with some areas prioritizing it more than others. To understand the diversity of local media response to the crisis, this study analyzed news content from 391 US newspapers with a combined circulation of 1554 areas. By examining the volume and composition of articles related to COVID-19, the study uncovered patterns influenced by population density, political orientation, and existing health infrastructure in these areas. The findings also indicated that local media initially focused on the human impact of the pandemic before later devoting more attention to broader economic and political implications. Conversely, national media maintained a consistent balance of COVID-related and non-COVID coverage throughout the study period without exhibiting similar area-specific patterns. Overall, the study's insights into local media response to the pandemic shed light on the significant role that geography and media diversity play in shaping public opinion and health outcomes during crises. The study's results may also be used to inform policy and practice aimed at promoting accurate public health communication and mitigating the pandemic's economic and social toll. The proposed method can be trained alongside other neural network components and provides accurate predictions at higher data counts with little additional computational cost. This method also demonstrates potential in stabilizing the training process for tasks involving large-scale image classification. With a processing power equivalent to about 5-7 regular batch sizes, this method accurately predicts the test accuracies, thereby offering a useful tool for guiding model selection and predicting performance at different scale. This paper introduces xor filters, a variant of Bloom filters constructed from xor operations, and examines their performance alongside standard Bloom filters. While xor filters allow for the use of lower-entropy hash functions, such as low-xor or LXOR, at the expense of slightly increased memory usage, they also support the use of more efficient high-xor or	HX at virtually no additional memory cost, making them a speed-optimal alternative. Experimentation with real-world datasets has yielded notable results, with xor filters requiring roughly 1.25 to 1.7 times more memory to match Bloom filter speeds, although they can be approximately 4 to 11 times faster while requiring only half to three times fewer bits per item. Additionally, xor filters can be approximately 4 to 11 times more memory-efficient than hyperlogarithmic filters, a type of approximate membership query data structure. The debate about how much of market history to consider remains unresolved. On one hand, the "nothing beats five minutes" theory suggests that recent market activity provides the most valuable insight, while on the other hand, some experts believe that past trends can offer beneficial guidance. In this research, we take a different approach and automatically determine the optimal time frame for market direction from historical price data. Unlike traditional methods that rely on human intuition, our network-based approach places transaction data at its core and generates the time scale dynamically. By operating in a distributed environment, we found that the most prominent trading activity on Amazon emerges around 15 minutes after the market opens, a period that is also marked by high transaction volume and distinct price fluctuations. Conversely, the EMH-driven daily time scale is characterized by more uniform trading activity. Similarly effective results were achieved for Yahoo stock market data, where our approach identified 20 minutes as the suitable time scale. When tested against a range of alternative time scales, our approach consistently outperformed them by accurately detecting market trends up to 15 minutes ahead while surpassing the performance of more established methods on yield prediction. Moreover, by integrating market history, we discovered that the most influential transactions are those that occur around 10% of the way into the time scale, a period marked by relatively high transaction volume and substantial price movements. In contrast, the least influential transactions are those that occur either very early or very late in this period. In total, our research successfully determined the optimal time scales for market direction from historical price data, a challenge that has long been a subject of human judgment and intuition. By integrating market history, we uncovered the relative importance of individual transactions, a factor that previous studies have overlooked. In addition to their potential to process real-time market data automatically, the advantages of our approach include its ability to handle large volumes of transaction data quickly and selectively focus on periods of significant market activity. In contrast, the traditional approaches of either fixed or dynamic time scales often fail to account for transaction volume, a factor that previous studies have disregarded in favor of a more uniform time scale. In total, the network-based time scales of our study offer an improved solution to the problem of market direction from historical price data. Existing solutions for rectifying biased models typically rely on supplementary data or rely on a central authority to assess model accuracy, but these require access to private information and can be costly.  Our innovative solution, FLVoogd, is the first federated learning system capable of producing reliable clusters without compromising sensitive personal information and prevents malicious data from influencing the model.  It utilizes a novel combination of efficient statistical learning methods and a trusted kernel function to identify anomalies on individual nodes, thereby preventing flawed data from entering the shared model. The atmospheric retention of a planet's gases is highly dependent on its mass, with more massive planets holding onto their atmosphere and smaller ones losing it to space. This concept was initially explored by Hart (1979) and further developed by other researchers, including Lammer et al. (2003) and Guillot-Deudney et al. (2019), who studied the atmospheric properties of small and massive Earth-sized planets. This study builds on previous work by investigating the atmospheric compositions of planets with masses ranging from those of a few to over 10 times that of our Earth. The research focuses on temperate planets with suitable conditions for liquid water, which is essential for life's presence, past, present, or future. The models used in this study differ from those of previous researchers in their inclusion of atmospheric interactions with solar wind and the magnetic properties of gases. The results of the computations for various planetary masses and atmospheric sizes show a transition from massive, completely internal atmospheres to minimal, extensively lost gases as the planet's mass decreases. The atmospheres of small planets tend to have less carbon dioxide but similar levels of molecular nitrogen compared to their larger counterparts. The transition from internal to external atmospheric control also sees an increase in the ratio of carbon to nitrogen gases. The loss of gases to space in smaller planets is further investigated through the examination of escape mechanisms, particularly the role of shock processes, which is more significant for more massive and less internally heated planets. The atmospheric properties of planets with masses similar to that of our Earth are largely unaffected by the presence of internal heat. The study also discovered that planets with masses similar to that of our Earth and those that are substantially more massive experience atmospheric escape that is balanced by volcanic outgassing. The incorporation of atmospheric interactions with solar wind and the magnetic properties of gases has significant implications for the atmospheric retention and composition of small and massive Earth-sized planets. The results of this research have important implications for future missions aimed at detecting small and massive Earth-sized planets, which will be focused on planets with masses similar to that of our Earth. The discovery that small planets tend to have less carbon dioxide but similar levels of molecular nitrogen compared to their larger counterparts suggests that future missions should aim to detect carbon dioxide and other atmospheric species that are easily detectable and may serve as indicators of potential biosignatures. The results of this study also highlight the significance of considering atmospheric escape mechanisms, particularly shock processes, in the modeling of atmospheres in massive Earth-sized planets. The significant challenge in scene text recognition lies in dealing with out-of-vocabulary words, especially those containing long unconventional characters. Current top-ranking models exhibit poor performance in identifying words that do not exist in their trained vocabulary. In order to overcome this issue, our research introduces a comprehensive out-of-vocabulary dataset that mimics real-world scenarios with unconventional words and also addresses the issue of word dropout. By using this dataset, we enhance the existing top models and successfully boost their accuracy. Furthermore, our research also showcases the potential of combining semantic ranking loss techniques and character attention to substantially enhance the overall performance of scene text recognition models. The proposed approach exhibits exceptional performance on the Scene Text Beyond OCR (STB) dataset, achieving remarkable accuracy of 80.95% and Meso-NME of 5.40% in a single model. Lastly, the heroku hosted model can be accessed via the link https://stb-model.herokuapp.com/. By using the STB Character-Level Benchmark, we demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly enhances the robustness of scene text recognition models in dealing with out-of-vocabulary words. Machine learning models greatly benefit from being trained with large datasets of labeled information. Yet, the process of acquiring these labeled data can be lengthy, expensive, or resource-intensive if done through crowd-sourcing. A technique known as selective labeling seeks to mitigate these costs by only requesting labels for specific, potentially costly instances. However, the challenge with selective labeling lies in determining which instances require labeling. Our research examines the problem of which instances to label, presenting two approaches to achieve this. The first, which instances to label, is formulated as a Markov Decision Process, which is efficient but requires prior knowledge of the model's parameters. Our alternative solution draws on the idea of informative instances, training a model to predict which instances are most informative prior to training on labeled data. Our experiments, conducted across seven datasets, reveal that both methods are beneficial, with the informative instances approach offering a more adaptable solution that outperforms the MDP-based method in classification tasks. The findings highlight the effectiveness of these methods in reducing the cost of acquiring labeled data through selective labeling. Our approach, implemented in code, can be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/ashish111/Selective_Labeling. Using theoretical calculations of the density of states and surface band structure, our analysis reveals that the ferromagnetic insulator EuS exhibits a particular realization of charge transfer across the interface that could be attributed to dispersed states at the InAs valence band maximum. These states ensure that the ferroelectric distortion of the interface is minimal. Furthermore, our results show that the growth of EuS on InAs preserves a C4 rotational symmetry, and by comparing with existing experimental data, our findings suggest the presence of an internal spin clock at the interface, which could be verified through spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. This research thus lays the groundwork for developing advanced spin-tripod technology by combining ferromagnetism, semiconductivity, and spin-orbit coupling. To balance computational efficiency with performance, researchers use pruning to reduce the complexity of large models. However, finding the optimal pruning schedule remains a significant challenge. Current approaches either rely on iterative processes or make assumptions about how to remove model components optimally. In contrast, we focus on grasping the underlying dynamics of a pre-pruned model to improve its performance. We introduced ClickTrain, a method that uses counterfactual explanations to determine which model parts should be unpruned. By treating the model as a black box and using examples of poor predictions it makes along with their corrected versions, ClickTrain generates unpruning plans. These plans prove effective, with results showing that unpruning weights previously thought unimportant can significantly improve model accuracy. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet reveal that ClickTrain yields better performance than existing pruning strategies and is capable of tackling tasks with multiple classes. The associated code is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/hughhuang1999/ClickTrain. ClickTrain has been successfully implemented and demonstrates superior performance over existing strategies in a range of tasks. The model's accuracy surpasses that of alternative approaches by as much as 11.44%, as evidenced by its performance on the ImageNet dataset. ClickTrain also proves scalable, yielding reliable results on various models and tasks. Furthermore, the concepts underlying ClickTrain are applicable to other model redesign tasks. We explore the potential of using ClickTrain in modifying model architectures. By treating the model's design as a black box, ClickTrain generates plans to alter network structures. These plans prove more effective than current approaches, yielding a performance boost of 2.17% for a modified ResNet on CIFAR-10 and 2.24% for a modified Vision Transformer on ImageNet. In conclusion, ClickTrain represents a groundbreaking solution for tackling unpruning challenges. Its unique combination of black-box grasping and counterfactual explanations enables the identification of optimal unpruning plans. As a versatile tool, ClickTrain is capable of targeting various models and tasks. Moreover, its concepts can be applied to other high-level model redesign tasks, as evident from its improved performance in altering network structures. Our work extends their results to an arbitrary multi-modal context and incorporates the fuzzy properties of associativity and commutativity. This enables us to derive a axiomatization for the resulting logic and establish its completeness using the fuzzy relation algebra as a semantics system. Furthermore, we examine various decidable sub-families of the proposed logic and establish their completeness with respect to both the fuzzy relation algebra and the standard Kripke frame semantics. By incorporating the fuzzy version of the cut rule, we also demonstrate that the fuzzy modal logic corresponding to any substructural modal logic is a conservative extension of that same logic. Moreover, we utilize the fuzzy relation algebra to separate the axioms associated with the various substructural modal logics, thereby providing a streamlined axiomatization for each of these logics. Lastly, we apply the fuzzy relation algebra method to derive the axioms for the fibring of substructural modal logics. This approach offers a novel and useful technique for introducing new axioms to substructural modal logics. Quantifying the propagation of diseases within a networked population is a key aspect of epidemiology. In this study, we examined a fundamental model for disease spread and developed a measure for predicting its progression across different population configurations. This measure, derived from the network's structure, reveals varying levels of predictability depending on the disease-triggering risks and the network's bridging roles. By applying this measure, we evaluated numerous real-world transportation systems and found significant associations between network fragility, epidemic spread and contagion patterns. Furthermore, our results suggested that specific network substructures, characterized by highly connected nodes with extensive connections to other parts of the network, significantly influence epidemic propagation and mortality rates. Ultimately, our research highlights the potential for employing network structure to make non-conditionally probabilistic predictions about disease spread and mortality rates based on disease-triggering probabilities and the network's structural characteristics. Our findings are further exemplified through an analysis of the US air transportation system and the COVID-19 pandemic. Lastly, we investigated the practical limitations of our model, discussing its general applicability, the scope for error in our predictive measure and the implications of individual behavior on disease propagation and our ability to make predictive statements about public health policy. Specifically, we examine a functional equation involving functions from the space $M_{\phi}^{(m)}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ which is homeomorphic to the adic solenoid $\omega_{\phi}^{(m)}$. The solution requires the use of p-adic-valued meromorphic functions of the form $\frac{F_{\phi,\lambda}^{(m)}}{E_{\phi,\lambda}^{(m)}}$, where $E_{\phi,\lambda}^{(m)}$ is a family of adic analytic functions defined in terms of the equation $\lambda^{\frac{m}{d}}E_{\phi,\lambda}^{(m)}(\zeta)=\phi(\lambda)\zeta^{m}$. Our results demonstrate that this equation has distinct solutions for different residue classes of $\lambda \bmod p^{n}$, and that the solutions exhibit periodic behavior as $n$ increases. We define a continuous action of the group $\Delta_{p,s}$ on the space $M_{\phi}^{(m)}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$, and show that the fiber over a fixed residue class $s \bmod p^{n}$ is invariant under this action. This paper outlines SATIN, a neural network-based approach for detecting abusive content in tweets through a unique representation of the text that incorporates both its meaning and the emotions expressed. SATIN employs a multi-layer model that uses various methods to learn its components. The first layer relies on pre-trained networks that convert English into a universal space and identify key phrases. The second layer combines the results of these two functions with a network that identifies emotions. The final layer is a binary classifier trained to predict abusive content. Experiments were conducted on the SemEval 2019 English Abuse Detection dataset and the results show that SATIN achieved a macro F1 score of 0.75 for detecting abusive content. Furthermore, in a post-evaluation study, we demonstrated that SATIN's performance improved when it was trained on a dataset of affective tweets, indicating that the system's ability to understand the emotions expressed improved from 0.49 to 0.65. Notably, SATIN's emotion identification module was found to be the most significant contribution to the system's overall performance. Additionally, in a further study, we found that by using a set of rules to automatically classify abusive content, we were able to increase the system's accuracy on that task by 0.07 points. The benefits of SATIN's use of a meaning-first approach, where it focuses on understanding the meaning of a tweet before attempting to determine its emotional content, were also formally confirmed in this study, as well as the system's ability to use a combination of linguistic features and the emotions expressed within a tweet to improve its accuracy in detecting abusive content. The benefits of using a more nuanced approach to classifying abusive content were also formally confirmed in this study. Previous studies have explored Bayesian Program Learning for generating handwriting, but a fundamental question remained unanswered: can a well-trained Bayesian program consistently produce high-quality handwriting even when it's based on limited and noisy data? Our investigation not only addresses this question but also showcases the exceptional versatility of Bayesian Program Learning by seamlessly adapting it to the generation of natural images. By formulating both tasks as distinct program spaces and employing a novel inference approach for exploring these spaces, we successfully demonstrated the feasibility of Bayesian Program Learning for image generation. Our results reveal that a Bayesian program trained in silo can create effective handwriting with just one training example, and when given ten examples, it produces handwriting indistinguishable from that of humans. Crucially, these benefits come without compromising its ability to generalize to novel conditions. Similarly, our system for generating natural images yields superior results compared to recent baseline methods, and when paired with pre-trained network features, it achieves image quality on par with the top Tiered-CNN baseline methods. A key advantage of our Bayesian Program Learning approach is its capacity for explainatory, interpretable generative processes. As a result, the generated handwriting and images are of remarkably high quality, and when analyzed, the underlying programs behind these samples reveal striking insights into what it takes to generate them. Moreover, the programs themselves are remarkably simple: the policy network for Bayesian Program Learning has a total of 248 parameters, making it an exceptionally efficient method for generating tasks as diverse as handwriting and image generation. A novel storage approach is proposed to efficiently retain information about the three-nucleon interaction without decomposing it into polynomial form. Instead of using polynomials with up to the ninth degree, our method utilizes structured arrays to store three-nucleon interaction matrix elements, which can be obtained through a range of quantum Monte Carlo calculations. These arrays comprise 15-dimensional vectors, representing the linear combinations of nine elementary operators applied to nine-dimensional vectors representing nucleon momenta. The approach allows for precise reconstruction of the interaction without polynomial decomposition and significantly reduces memory requirements for computational tasks that handle the complete nuclear interaction up to the three-nucleon level. Our analysis demonstrates that, even with the exclusion of certain high-momentum three-nucleon interactions, the proposed storage method excels in efficiency compared to polynomial decomposition. Furthermore, our findings indicate that storing the complete three-nucleon interaction with this storage scheme leads to a considerable reduction in memory requirements from approximately $1.1 \times 10^{5}$ to $1.2 \times 10^{4}$ terabytes. The development of this storage method facilitates the thorough calculation of the three-nucleon interaction and lays the groundwork for an extensive, high-precision database of the complete nuclear interaction. Moreover, our work has far-reaching implications for applying similar strategies to calculate higher-order many-nucleon interactions and other complex quantum systems. Lastly, our method can also be adapted for use in quantum chemistry, particularly in the context of traditional computational methods limited by memory constraints where high-precision wave function evaluations on large grids are concerned. The presented scheme is versatile and suitable for use in computational methods limited by memory constraints where high-precision wave function evaluations on large grids are concerned. The widespread use of Deep Neural Networks has led to a significant increase in the adoption of GPU computing for academic and industrial purposes. While advancements have been made in optimizing inference performance, training processes remain underserved. Memory management during deep learning training is typically handled by a allocator that facilitates data movement between the CPU and GPU. Past optimization efforts have failed to address memory allocation on GPUs, leaving room for potential improvements in memory usage and performance. In response, we introduce DynaSOAr, a sophisticated memory allocator tailored for deep learning workloads on GPUs. By integrating a stack-based memory allocation approach and employing a dynamic memory pool strategy, DynaSOAr exhibits superior performance and efficiency. Compared to the standard CUDA allocator, DynaSOAr's sequential allocation time reaches speeds up to 150 times faster while reducing memory overhead by a factor of 10. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's optimal memory allocation leads to a 5% average computation time reduction on various benchmark models, along with a 10% decrease in memory usage. Our results demonstrate that DynaSOAr's enhanced memory management results in substantial performance and efficiency gains. On a large scale of about 100 parsecs, the density is significantly anisotropic, with a strong line dividing the area into two parts. As we move to smaller scales, the density becomes less anisotropic, with its main anisotropic feature remaining the line running along the line dividing the area. The quantum scissors technique in combination with differential gain switching enables the creation of multiplexed entangled states of polarized photons. By manipulating a beam splitter and adjusting the relative delays and phases, intricate entanglements of three, four, five, six, and eight photons have been achieved. Furthermore, calculations indicate an extremely high fidelity in the generated entangled states, surpassing 99% for systems of three and four photons. The application of these complex entangled states in quantum computation and quantum teleportation is also explored. Additionally, the approach of using scissors in the quantum realm demonstrates an innovative method for engineering intricate photonic states. The findings of this research facilitate advancements in the efficient generation of entangled photons for both optical and quantum comb-based quantum information technologies. The described setup may be adapted for free-space optical comms by incorporating additional alignment-insensitive components. The quantum scissors method offers an adaptable tool for the preparation of entangled states, showcasing its potential in the quantum information sciences. The detailed characterization of the generated entangled states using quantum tomography is also presented, showcasing the versatility of the quantum scissors technique in the quantum information sciences. The research has the potential to be expanded to larger-scale entangled states, thereby enhancing our understanding of quantum physics and its applications, also known as quantum physics and its applications. The research is also attached as EMB C-2020-07. The source code for the quantum scissors technique is available at https://github.com/emb-c-2020-07/quantum-scissors, the experimental setup documentation can be found at https://emb-c-2020-07.github.io/quantum-scissors/README.html, and the associated data can be accessed via https://emb-c-2020-07.github.io/quantum-scissors/data.html. To prevent IoT device attacks through misclassification, we introduce a cost-aware classification framework that considers risk and cost factors. Our research reveals that traditional least square loss functions produce overly confident misclassified predictions, which can increase the device's vulnerability to attacks when losses are disproportionately distributed. We define a novel risk metric for misclassification, utilizing both predictive density and posterior probability, and demonstrate that replacing the least square loss with our risk-based approach and combining them yields better classification performance and increased security against attacks in uneven loss scenarios. Our proposed method holds significant potential for securing IoT devices against malicious activities facilitated by misclassification. All code is available at https://github.com/stuarrystore/crc. Experimental results validate the theoretical findings and show the method's superiority in practical applications. For example, in the Google M4 competition, our method achieved a 5.3% improvement in MAE with a 99.97% success rate in binary classification within 100 trials. We also analyze the method's performance in real-world datasets and discuss its suitability for production use. All source code is accessible at https://github.com/stuarrystore/crc. Our method has the potential to be implemented in IoT device classification services, which could significantly lower the impact of attacks and accidents caused by misclassification. For example, in the Google M4 competition, our method achieved a 5.3% improvement in MAE with a 99.97% success rate in binary classification within 100 trials. Our approach is versatile and can be applied in various classification tasks by adjusting the risk metric according to the problem's specific requirements. To promote the method's security and usability, we suggest integrating it into the IoT device classification services, which could lead to a substantial reduction in attacks and accidents caused by misclassification. Our research is the first to incorporate risk into the classification of IoT devices and, through theoretical analysis and experimental results, demonstrates its potential to improve performance and security. We respond to concerns around the method's computationally intensive nature by noting that the cost of computing our proposal is comparable to traditional least square loss functions. To mitigate potential performance degradation in the presence of noisy labels, we suggest utilizing the method in conjunction with semi-supervised learning, which has been successfully applied in the Google M4 competition. We acknowledge a recent paper's contribution to the classification of IoT devices, which reached a similar conclusion regarding the importance of risk, but note that our research makes a more substantial contribution through the incorporation of cost factors and the development of a new loss function. Previous research often evaluated aligners in an unsupervised learning setting, where they were trained with a tiny fraction of the Wikipedia corpus, typically 10 million tokens. Despite this, these aligners were expected to perform just as well on larger, more diverse datasets such as the German subsection of the Wikipedia-Arabic dataset, which contains roughly 1 billion tokens. In contrast, our study reveals that an aligner trained on a modest collection of 50 million tokens within the Wikipedia-Arabic dataset yields superior results compared to established tools like GIZA++ and its efficient counterpart, fastalign. Moreover, our aligner's performance surpasses that of non-parametric approaches like bitext-aligner and the Wikipedia-based aligners previously proposed by Adel and Alon, both of which also operated within the 10 million token mark. Our research further demonstrates that our aligner's accuracy can be enhanced through the utilization of two distinct forms of supervision: targeted training and data augmentation employing a novel, semi-supervised training method we've devised. When trained with as little as 50 million tokens, our aligner surpasses state-of-the-art models in terms of sentence alignment quality within the Wikipedia-Arabic dataset, a standard benchmark in the field. Our study also explores how the proposed aligner scales with increasing corpus sizes, evaluating its performance at multiple milestones along the way. In addition, we've developed an open-source tool for evaluating sentence aligners, which is now freely accessible on GitHub under the name fastalign++. Our results reveal that our aligner exhibits a unique combination of high performance and efficient training capabilities. In particular, at the 50 million token mark, our aligner is both the fastest to train and the most efficient in terms of the memory it occupies, often training 30% to 100% faster and using 5% to 50% fewer resources than other aligners in the process. In order to facilitate further study, we've made our source code, the fastalign++ tool, and the Wikipedia-Arabic dataset publicly available on GitHub under the name fastalign++. In addition, our study, which is entitled 'Evaluating Sentence Aligners within Wikipedia-Arabic', is now freely accessible on arXiv at the link provided. This paper presents a novel asynchronous algorithm derived from the block-iterative decomposition method, specifically formulated to address nonlocal generalized asymptotic decay in relativistic scattering theory. Grounded in the functional analysis framework, the theoretical justification of the algorithm's convergence is achieved by leveraging the semi-convergence principle. By applying this method to solve the Klein-Gordon equation on a fixed energy level, we successfully obtained solutions exhibiting generalized asymptotic decay near the absolute continuous spectrum. Moreover, our method has the advantage of withholding the requirement for synchronous updates in the communication process, thus rendering it suitable for large-scale computations. The Klein-Gordon equation is a fundamental model in the field of relativistic scattering theory, so our solution has far-reaching implications in this area. Additionally, the Klein-Gordon equation is also an effective mathematical model for studying damped harmonic oscillations in the relativistic regime. The presented asynchronous algorithm is likely to be the first of its kind to address generalized asymptotic decay in relativistic scattering theory. Classical mathematical operations like differentiation and integration have inherent relationships with harmonic functions that exhibit positive definiteness. This property is maintained regardless of the dimensionality of these functions. This study extends the concept of positive definiteness to a specific class of functions called zonal functions, and explores its implications on Cartesian products of spaces with positive definite functions. Specifically, it is demonstrated that differentiating or integrating zonal functions at center results in a new property called almost positive definiteness. This almost positive definiteness can be further generalized to Cartesians products of spaces with almost positive definite functions. To validate the concept of almost positive definiteness, this study provides criteria for verifying its presence on particular spaces, including the examples of spaces of square summable sequences and Hardy spaces. These examples also illustrate that positive definiteness is not simply a consequence of almost positive definiteness. Finally, the study examines the relationship between positive definite and almost positive definite functions in various spaces, including those mentioned above. This study presents new perspectives on the classical mathematical operations of differentiation and integration, and sheds light on the broader theory of positive definite functions. It also paves the way for potential applications in fields like engineering, medical research, and political science. In addition, the study provides insights into the computational methods of positive definite kernel functions and zonal function representations. These computational methods have practical applications in fields like computer science, geography, law, medicine, and social sciences. Furthermore, the study offers agglomerative clustering algorithms based on positive definite kernel functions and zonal function representations. These algorithms have real world applications in fields like computer science, geography, law, medicine, and social sciences. Lastly, the study extends the concept of positive definite kernel functions to higher dimensional functions and provides new classification algorithms as a result. The dynamics of liquid foams are heavily influenced by the surface roughness of the bubbles. This effect is quantified by the roughness factor, which is established as a dimensionless measure of the energy related to surface roughness. It's shown that this factor determines the flow's 1D state, specifically the ratio of the energies associated with bubble formation and surface tension. When the factor in question exceeds a certain threshold, the foam displays characteristics of a jammed, solid material with a non-zero yield stress. This relationship between roughness factor and jamming is akin to that between density and jamming in packs of rigid particles. Additionally, the jamming transition in foams is contingent upon the process's history, much like in packs of hard particles. Lastly, the jamming transition in foams is found to be hypersensitive to the presence of surface defects. This behavior is seen as a consequence of the crossover from a disordered, jammed state to a highly ordered, metastable state accompanied by a dramatic reduction in volume. The jamming transition in foams is thus proposed to be an example of a thermodynamic transition akin to melting or boiling. The jamming transition in foams is also compared to the glass transition in supercooled liquids. Both transitions are characterized by a collective overloading of the material's inherent structural defects. Similarly, the jamming transition in foams involves a sudden and intense loading of the materials' surface defects. The exclusion of these surface defects from the material's jammed, solid state is likened to the exclusion of freezier clusters in the formation of a jammed, solid ice. The structural differences between jammed, solid foams and jammed, solid ice are proposed to be a consequence of the optimization of respective structural components, akin to the behavior observed in packs of hard particles. The jamming transition in foams is thus proposed to represent a prototypical example of a structural phase transition with characteristics drawn from the behavior of liquids, glasses, and solids. Lastly, the jamming transition in foams is found to be accompanied by a colossal decrease in the material's coefficient of thermal expansion. This effect is most pronounced in the material's near-jammed, solid state and is proposed to be a consequence of the presence of long-waving, thermally induced surface undulations that contribute to the material's surface roughness. Our study reveals a substantial mass enhancement of dipolar electron-hole excitations in sodium when it is in a metallic state near the M point, exhibiting enhancement of roughly three times that seen with monopole hole excitations at the same location. This significant mass effect influences the quasiparticle resonance of the dipolar electron-hole interaction, causing it to be prominent at an energy of about 14 meV above the Fermi level. This condition allows the quasiparticle lifetime to be significantly shortened to roughly half of its value at lower energies. This significant shortening of the lifetime by dipolar interactions rivals the impact that monopole interactions have on the same process in sodium. Moreover, the pairing of these electron-hole pairs through a dynamically-induced force contributes to the stability of the $^3S_1$ triplet superconductor in this material, potentially outweighing the suppression of pairing that arises from the interference with monopole pairs, thus indicating a potentially strong enhancement of the pairing through dipolar electron-hole pairs in sodium. This result suggests that dynamically-induced forces in metals with strong dipolar interactions like sodium deserve further investigation as potential mechanisms for novel types of superconducting materials. Furthermore, our study presents a detailed analysis of how the mass enhancement of dipolar electron-hole pairs in sodium comes to be, revealing the significant role that the long-range component of the Coulomb interaction plays in this process, despite its negative implications for the pairing of these pairs through a dynamically-induced force in the context of the $^3S_1$ triplet superconductor. This effect to be significant in other binary alkali metals as well. Additionally, our study also finds that the correlation between the frequency of the dipolar phonons and the quasiparticle resonance of the electron-hole pairs is significantly shortened, becoming about ten times lower than expected. This analysis builds upon the theoretical framework of dual-density functional theory, further develops it by considering the constraint of inhomogeneous density, while also incorporating the effects of wave-vector dependent amplitude and phase uncertainty for the pairing function through the use of the phase-functional approach within the Hedin's double-time Green's function formalism. The details of our computational method are provided in the supporting documents. In contrast, the long-term behavior of the system is determined by the second of these oscillating components, resulting in a single, self-contained wave of oscillation traveling along the chain. To analyze the primordial non-Gaussian signatures of these features, we create two tailored tools: the Field Variation Effect (FVE) measure, which quantifies their impact, and the Order-Weighted measure (OWE), which measures the magnitude within the non-Gaussian signature landscape. By applying these tools, we identify a critical relationship between the features' locations, widths, and the order in which they occur, and we show that a limited number of significant features can produce a substantial non-Gaussian signature at third order. Furthermore, we find that these features' contributions can be large even when the feature only affects the second-order signature at a secondary order. Our results imply that a comprehensive analysis of the cosmic microwave background and future surveys like COSMOD and Primordial Non-Gaussianity Experiment may be able to detect these features using the bispectrum and hexabicross. Moreover, we propose a detection strategy for these features that involves measuring their relative orientation within the feature region to a precision of at least 10%. Our findings are in line with previous studies on abrupt changes within inflationary models, and we also discuss their implications for model-building. Ultimately, we conclude that a comprehensive survey of the cosmic microwave background may be able to detect these features using the bispectrum, and a measurement precision of at least 10% on the relative orientation of these features could reveal the existence of multiple features. Additionally, future surveys like COSMOD and Primordial Non-Gaussianity Experiment may be able to detect these features using the hexabicross with an angle precision of at least 20%. Furthermore, we also found that the predicted hexabicross can distinguish between different single-field inflationary models that have similar predicted signatures for the bispectrum. Deep learning models are widely regarded as exemplary predictive models, yet they suffer from limitations that can be overcome by quantifying their uncertainties. By treating their output as sampling from a distribution rather than a fixed point, researchers aim to measure the confidence level of predictions. This approach is known as Bayesian deep learning, but it presents significant challenges, notably the intractability of computing the posterior distribution via Bayes' theorem. This difficulty is compounded in the case of non-convex parameters and observations. Despite these obstacles, researchers have developed methods for approximating the predictive distribution, but the efficacy of these attempts has not been extensively evaluated. This study aims to rectify this oversight by comparing various Bayesian deep learning methods for generating posterior samples, evaluating their performance across multiple benchmarks in terms of their alignment with the true posterior distribution. By shedding light on the merits and shortcomings of these methods, we seek to facilitate informed method selection. Furthermore, we have developed the BLIP toolkit, a comprehensive software package that facilitates the computation of the predictive distribution for complex models. This toolkit is accessible through the following repository: https://github.com/continuous-bayes/BLIP. In future work, we intend to apply these methods to the construction of the predictive distribution in the context of reinforcement learning, aiming to quantify the exploratory benefits of uncertainty-driven sampling in the sampling distribution. This research is an extension of our previous conference paper, significantly expanding on the presented material. In particular, we have added a novel method for approximating the posterior distribution known as "BLIP," established a formal connection between maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian inference, incorporated both theoretical and empirical analyses of the performance of ML-BLIP, and addressed criticisms of the initial paper through a point-by-point rebuttal. Additionally, we have updated the methodology section to clarify the differences between various methods for computing the predictive distribution. Lastly, we have added a new section on future work, where we explore the potential applications and adaptations of our methods for computing the predictive distribution. These potential avenues of research could themselves be the subjects of future investigation and are worth pursuing in the event of future opportunities. In addition to these updates, we now provide the code for our methods in the BLIP toolkit (https://github.com/continuous-bayes/BLIP), a comprehensive software package that facilitates the computation of the predictive distribution for complex models. This code is fully documented in Section 7 and is an integral component of our research. Furthermore, we have maintained a separate repository for our paper, where the slides and figures can be viewed

Research into dark matter models that involve the splitting of dark matter masses has gained interest due to its implications on dark matter-nucleon scattering, especially in relation to events like the iconic $J/\psi$ missing-energy observation by the DAMA collaboration. A previous study in arXiv:1906.03323 demonstrated that this model can be compatible with constraints from other experiments when considering only visible $J/\psi$ decays, but due to the potential for $J/\psi$ decay into invisible modes, which have a higher cross-section than visible decays in certain mass ranges. Hence, re-evaluations of invisible decay limits from other experiments, such as XENON100 and LUX, are necessary. This is addressed in a new study, which combines these new limits with constraints from dark matter direct detection experiments to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the parameter space of the $(J/\psi, \chi)$ decomposition model. While the visible and invisible decay analyses yield similar constraints for the visible case, the invisible decay limits prove to be more stringent in the non-relativistic mass range. Furthermore, taking into account the potential for future XENONnT upgrades to reach single-event sensitivities of $10^{-13}~\rm{pc/cm^2}$, as well as other planned dark matter direct detection experiments, could significantly restrict the suitable mass range for dark matter-nucleon scattering in this model. However, it is essential to note that the $J/\psi$ decay into invisible modes introduces novel constraints, especially in the heavy mass range of approximately $10^{-12}~\rm{pc/cm^2}$, which has significant implications for future multi-ton dark matter direct detection experiments, where even the heaviest mass ranges in the model could still be within reach. Lastly, the model's $J/\psi$ decay into invisible modes also raises concerns that future multi-ton dark matter direct detection experiments could be sensitive to regions of the parameter space that violate lepton flavor conservation principles, a critical ethical consideration, thus necessitating future
multi-ton dark matter direct detection experiments to carefully examine their capacity for this model's parameter space, especially in regions that may breach conservation principles or remain undetected by current experiments.} \end{abstract}

Minimal videos, comprising basic movements and short, concise scenes, can
illuminate our understanding of human dynamic vision and perception capabilities
and have direct applications in expert systems. One way to create these videos
is by manipulating atomic motion units in existing videos. Another approach is to
directly optimize them through machine learning algorithms. Our proposed method
combines both techniques, leveraging pre-trained atomic motion detectors and
optimal segmentation algorithms based on reinforcement learning environments.
This method excels at finding minimal videos that convey expert-labeled key frame
characteristics under constrained temporal limitations. Furthermore, minimal
videos created using our method demonstrate higher similarity scores in expert-
to-user evaluation compared to videos generated through alternative methods. 
Our source code and a demo are available at https://github.com/snguyen-vt/minimal-video-learning. 
In terms of performance, minimal videos obtained using our method have comparable
inferences to state-of-the-art models in the solar vehicle dataset of the DetNet
challenge. This represents a key finding as optimal inference often requires
subsequent post-processing processing to comply with DetNet constraints. As a
result, minimal videos created using our method offer an appealing balance of
compactness, ease of deployment, and high classification accuracy. 
To promote research in this field, we introduce a new benchmark called
Minimal Videos for Vision, available at https://minimalvideoforvision.com/. 
This comprehensive resource includes the dataset of minimal videos created using our
method using the COCO dataset and an evaluation framework that facilitates
comparisons to existing approaches. 
Our method is an open-source solution available at https://github.com/snguyen-vt/minimal-video-ml. 
As the field evolves, the concept of minimal videos can be applied to various
domains such as video editing, filmmaking, broadcast media, visual arts, and
more. Ultimately, the idea of minimal videos can facilitate collaborative
efforts between human experts and machine learning algorithms to produce compact,
effective, and engaging videos.

Government under the National Science Foundation's Grant 2034618. 
The images used in this research were sourced from ImageNet. 
All video creation experiments were conducted using a 24GB RAM NVIDIA
GeForce RTX 3080Ti graphics card.

By distributing adjusted adjustment factors for satellite imagery across the globe, our study aims to facilitate fair evaluation and comparison of weather forecasting models by normalizing datasets to account for varying levels of illumination. We utilize multiple areas with consistent land use patterns, including built environments, natural landscapes, and water features, to derive adjustment factors that can rectify discrepancies caused by different lighting conditions in models trained with satellite images. We demonstrate the significance of normalizing datasets on examples such as Seattle, Chicago, and Miami through a comprehensive evaluation of forecast performance using the persistence model, revealing that applying our adjustment factors yields more accurate evaluations and avoids misleading inferences resulting from illumination biases. Furthermore, we make available a simple open-source method to calculate these adjustment factors, along with the adjusted data for the regions examined in our study. This approach is intended to be easily applied and adaptable for use with other datasets. We intend this resource to benefit researchers developing weather forecasting models, who may use it to compare existing models more fairly or develop new learning methods that produce more accurate and robust weather forecasts with wider general applicability. Our study, associated data, and code can be accessed at https://advancedresearch.microsoft.com/weather-normalization. In addition, the adjusted data and normalized satellite images are available to download at https://github.com/MRAG/WeatherNormalization. In contrast to existing fair learning techniques that we are not utilizing, our proposed approach addresses the concerns of dataset fairness by fair utilization rather than fair generation; it also addresses the challenges of bounded outcomes and fair group learning while emphasizing the significance of group fairness over individual fairness in the context of our study. Our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance when compared to existing weather forecasting methods, as evidenced by our experimental findings. In addition, the time required to calculate the adjustment factors is under one minute, making our approach highly efficient. In terms of computational overhead, the adjustment process incurs virtually no computational cost when compared to training the persistence model. Our proposed approach has far-reaching potential to benefit researchers working in weather forecasting, as well as those working in related areas such as reinforcement learning, explaining predictions, and model selection. Ultimately, the widespread adoption of the proposed approach has the potential to enhance the precision and robustness of weather forecasting models while promoting more accurate and fair evaluations of these models. In indirect dark matter detection experiments, the presence of CP violation can lead to a significant expansion in the mass range of dark matter candidates within the framework of three-Higgs-doublet models that have a strongly interacting nature. However, the majority of the additional parameter space, characterized by small CP-breaking parameters, is not accessible through future dark matter direct detection facilities. The anticipation is that the upcoming LHC run II and dark matter direct and indirect detection experiments will be able to explore the remainder of the parameter space. Nevertheless, the possibility of CP violation and its impact on the consistency of the electroweak symmetry remains unexplored in the three-Higgs-doublet models. In this research, the focus is on the interplay between the CP-breaking parameters and the oblique parameters, with an evaluation of the one-loop corrections to the oblique parameter S in three-Higgs-doublet models, incorporating both weakly interacting and heavily interacting dark matter scenarios. The outcomes reveal that, in the models where the dark matter does not couple to the Standard Model Higgs boson, S is largely insensitive to the CP-breaking parameters. However, when the dark matter does couple to the Standard Model Higgs boson, S becomes sensitive to the parameters that govern the CP-breaking interactions between the Higgs boson and the dark matter. The research also reveals that, in the heavily interacting dark matter scenario, the discrete symmetry that helps to eliminate the tree-level flavor-changing neutral currents also leads to a connection between the parameter that governs the CP-breaking interaction of the dark matter and the parameter that governs its coupling to the Standard Model Higgs boson. Banking fraud has escalated into a significant global issue. Most techniques addressing this problem are based on traditional graph theory, however the standard methods used to construct banking graphs have limitations, particularly in ensuring the final graph's validity. Valid banking graphs refer to those where every node has a consistent set of labels. In this research, we introduce the concept of generative valid banking graphs through the utilization of Graph Generative Network (GGN). Unlike existing methods that rely on arbitrary graph construction, the proposed GGN creates banking graphs with correct edges and nodes, thereby ensuring validity. Additionally, the proposed method learns features directly from the data in the form of a learned banking graph, thus demonstrating efficiency in training time. Our experiments involve evaluating the proposed method against existing methods in both valid and invalid graph contexts using five real-world datasets for classification tasks. Our results indicate that GGN surpasses the alternative methods in terms of accuracy, macro F-1 score and micro F-1 score, while also demonstrating a significant reduction in edge and node prediction errors. Our code is available at https://github.com/asharifi/GGN. Our findings suggest the potential of applying the GGN in other graph classification tasks due to its effectiveness. As a practical application, the valid banking graphs generated by the GGN can be utilized for semantic navigation in a virtual banking environment. Moreover, the learned features can be used for classification purposes, thus rendering an edge for the GGN. Our analysis on the GGN's predictive factors revealed the importance of node degree, in-degree, out-degree, node label, node position, node size, node color, node type, edge weight and edge navigation in classification tasks. Nevertheless, our results indicate that the predictive factors used in traditional methods are less significant than those used by the GGN. Our research on the GGN's robustness in relation to attacks on banking graphs, particularly in scenario of graph navigation attack, revealed the GGN's immunity to attacks that aim to manipulate graph structure in banking fraud detection. To enhance the robustness of self-training algorithms for parsing tasks, we introduce Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST), a novel approach that surpasses traditional self-training methods. By leveraging deep contextualized representations from pre-trained language models, DCST's self-training framework outperforms existing protocols. Furthermore, DCST's reliance on context-aware selection of examples and self-labelling minimizes the influence of noisy labels, allowing the model to yield context-specific improvements. DCST's effectiveness is demonstrated across various datasets, including the WAKeWB and Wikitonary datasets, where it exhibits superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, a detailed analysis of DCST's components and extensions highlights their individual efficacy in enhancing parsing capabilities. Furthermore, our research showcases the success of continued training on extraneous tasks using DCST, as exemplified by enhanced performance on the SST-2 dataset after training on a parsing task. I propose an approach to determining the fusion rules for non-trivial symmetries in field theories that defy inverse duplication. Building on the dual transformation concept established by Pickking and Tsuboi, I develop an integrated framework that simultaneously identifies both the symmetry algebra and the fusion rule for any given non-invertible symmetry. This framework is applied to $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric field theories, with a demonstration of its efficacy through analysis of the $E_6$ superconformal field theory. Additionally, I outline potential future applications of this approach.

We investigate the complexity of solving a linear equation system over a finite field, and find that its computationally hard cases can be formulated in a specific logical framework. This result enables us to reduce the complexity of solving quadratic equations over finite fields, a problem currently considered computationally hard. This reduction is done by translating the quadratic equation into a particular type of logical formula, thus connecting the quadratic problem to a well-defined logical theory. This connection strengthens our previous finding that solving linear equation systems over finite fields is computationally hard, as it is now proven to be so even under strict constraints on the equation system. This conclusion is further generalized to the solutions of these equation systems, and the results are discussed in terms of their implications for finite fields, the properties of which are of course trivially defined. In contrast to the finite field setting, we find that solving linear equation systems over the rational numbers does not have a corresponding logical representation, thus distinguishing it from its counterpart in the finite field setting. A non-transitive tuple would have the third card require a different ordering against the first two cards to follow the same pattern. We explored the likelihood of randomly selecting non-transitive 3-tuples and 5-tuples in a standard 52-card deck and found that both scenarios are highly probable, with the outcomes aligning with the predictions of Bernoulli trials. Additionally, the distributions associated with these outcomes closely resemble uniform distributions. Given that the concepts behind these patterns have analogues in the fields of mathematics and statistics, we referred to them as "universal patterns of discrepancy." The proliferation of configuration mechanisms in modern software enables
developers to tailor applications to diverse user preferences and environments.
However, this flexibility comes at a cost, as most software configurations
remain unused during execution, resulting in unnecessary computational overhead
and the potential for security vulnerabilities arising from unselected features.
Therefore, eliminating the unnecessary components that are part of the program
execution path is a defensible goal, as this can improve performance and reduce
security risks. Unfortunately, identifying and quantifying the impact of feature
interactions, which are often prevalent due to the multitude of configuration
options, adds an additional layer of complexity to the task. For the purpose of
this study, we examined the internal audit tool, Nessus, which is widely used in
the security community, with a view to exploring the strategies and challenges
associated with identifying and removing the options that are not used during
execution. Our investigation began by manually reviewing the internal audit tool,
Nessus, in order to understand its configuration mechanisms and the phenomena of
feature interaction. The results of our analysis revealed that the options
associated with the plugin's scheduled scan configuration are not used during
execution and that these options are involved in complex interactions with other
options. We then proposed a formal approach to identifying the options that are
not used during execution. Although this approach can be applied to a wide range of
configurable systems, we acknowledge that the practical implementation of this
method remains challenging due to issues such as partial observability and the
unpredictability of system traces. Therefore, an alternative heuristic approach
was devised to approximate the desired behavior, which involves simulating the
system traces and eliminating the options that are not visible during simulation.
Our experimental evaluation of this heuristic approach confirmed that it is capable
of removing the unused options from the plugin's scheduled scan configuration with
a high degree of accuracy. However, further work is needed to investigate the
applicability of our proposed strategies to other configurable systems and to assess
the effectiveness of the approach in reducing the complexity of feature interactions. 
Also, an additional area of research could be the integration of our proposed strategy
with the configuration validation techniques in order to ensure that the removal of
options does not break any existing invariants in the system. As a result, the revised
version of the software with the options removed would undergo formal verification
in order to guarantee that the constraints of the original system are maintained.

Assuming the interaction is dominated by spin-independent $\vec{\sigma} \cdot \vec{\sigma}$ and being scattered off of $^{16}$O nuclei in the sun, our calculations reveal significant ionization impacts on dark matter detection strategies. The photoelectric effect and electron-rocket mechanisms are identified as key processes influencing the current understanding of dark matter interactions. In contrast, a novel approach presented in this research utilizes a data-driven method to extract features from ECG signals, facilitating direct training of deep-learning models for complex ECG analysis tasks. The recent proliferation of very short-term video prediction has been driven
by technologies relying on highly efficient basic video prediction (BasicVSR).
Unfortunately, BasicVSR has inherent shortcomings in its capacity to learn
spatial structure information due to its reliance on a diagonal kernel, resulting
in noticeable reconstruction artifacts that are exacerbated by the repeated
interpolation of fine-grained predictions within basic video prediction.
  To address the issues mentioned above, we developed basic video prediction
with additional spatial information using half-framed (BasicVSR++), which
incorporates structure information through the utilization of a horizontal and
vertical kernel for predicting adjacent frames. In conjunction with the mid-frame
prediction feature, this kernel aids in accurately capturing spatial structure
information without necessitating explicit training for frames.
  We conducted a series of experiments using the mid-frame prediction feature in
conjunction with BasicVSR++, evaluating its performance using the PASCAL SMD,
KITTI2D, and TSM datasets. Our results indicate that BasicVSR++ surpasses basic
video prediction on the PASCAL SMD and KITTI2D datasets in terms of PSNR,
while significantly outperforming it on the TSM dataset in terms of SSIM and
visual aesthetics. Notably, BasicVSR++ superior performance comes at the cost
of reduced computational requirements, as measured in the number of operator
calls. Our proposed method, basic video prediction with additional spatial information using half-framed (BasicVSR++), boasts notable
computational efficiency improvements. Furthermore, our long-term goal is to
develop a basic video prediction algorithm with minimal computational overhead
while maintaining or surpassing state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy. Our code has been publicly released on the website https://yj9y9y9y9.github.io/BasicVSR++. Additionally, our video demonstrations can be accessed via the YouTube channel https://youtu.be/9GvXpW1ZXW8. Lastly, our project has been accepted to Oral presentation at the ICCV 2023 conference, where our results will be presented. Next, we will be discussing the evaluations conducted on the TSM dataset. In the evaluation, our BasicVSR++ method proved to be more efficient in terms of computational cost while also exhibiting a significant gain in structural aesthetics as measured using the PASCAL norms. In multiple-real-world applications, a robot often needs to perform various tasks on the same machine, and it's usually not possible to isolate different tasks from each other. Our research focuses on resolving issue overlap during multi-task reinforcement learning where tasks share the same environment. We find that even a simple, single model of a task-agnostic dynamics can cause previously learned tasks to decline in performance on those same tasks. We introduce a new technique, known as Model Orthogonization of Dynamics Models, which uses multiple models to monitor and learn from the variations in task performance under similar conditions and can effectively prevent task confusion. Our modeling approach uses variations in task execution as explanations for observed task interactions, leading to a generalizable and efficient method to separate tasks from each other. Long-term recurrent networks have shown efficacy in modeling long-range speech patterns, but their performance is hampered by a lack of insight into internal cascades. We address this limitation by developing a novel, cascaded network architecture that enhances long-term recurrent models with a deeper understanding of internal structures. In our proposed framework, a cascade of network blocks creates a cumulative, multi-stage recurrent network, allowing for the long-term representation of input data. We investigate several internal structures, including recurrent cascades with recurrent internal structures, and non-recurrent cascades with external structures. We evaluate their effectiveness on the TTS task and discover that a self-attention cascaded LSTMs framework exhibits a superior performance of 1.48 in scale in terms of the log-scale error metric on the VOICE BANK dataset. Furthermore, the model's additional computational complexity is found to be approximately 1.32 times that of a conventional LSTM. We conclude that our proposed framework represents a compelling solution for long-term signal modeling. Additionally, the framework offers a degree of interpretability not seen in previous deep learning architectures through the removal of redundant internal structures during training. As such, the model is a suitable choice for long-term signal representation and is suitable for a wide range of applications including speech analysis, text-to-speech, speech recognition, etc. – all of which often encounter periodic or quasi-periodic signals. We include a supplementary document with further details of the model's internal structures. We examine the effectiveness of our model in a text-to-speech synthesis task and discover that it yields a superior synthetic speech quality, as judged by human listeners, in comparison to a conventional deep LSTM model. Specifically, the model achieves a 35.76% increase in the QMOS ratings on the VOICE BANK dataset. We conclude that the enhanced representation of speech patterns in our model results in a more effective transfer of these patterns to the synthetic speech signals, thereby improving their overall quality. Finally, a classifier is applied to the stacked features for action classification. By simultaneously extracting rich features from data via opposing networks, BCAE serves as a highly effective data compression technique. Unlike traditional methods, this approach expands data while minimizing loss through comparison of transformed features. To evaluate the accuracy of our model, we compare its predictions with observed data from the Coma galaxy cluster. The age of information (AoI) is a measure of how up-to-date wireless communication users are. In contrast to typical throughput and energy efficiency research, which often rely on long-term averages, this paper's primary objective is to establish a lower bound for the AoI in wireless communication systems, taking into account the constraints of wireless packet transmission and a lossy discrete-time, time-varying, Bernoulli mixture channel. To achieve this goal, a nonconvex optimization problem is developed, where the objective is to maximize throughput and, subsequently, establish a lower bound for the AoI, utilizing the Lagrange duality technique. It is discovered that increased throughput results in a higher lower bound for the AoI and, through analytical analysis, the optimal power allocation for the AoI is determined for a range of scenarios, including when the channel follows a Bernoulli mixture and when it is completely unreliable. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that minimizing the AoI involves a trade-off with the system's reliability and that the optimal power allocation can be determined using the Lagrange dual values during stable operation or by prioritizing older users during outages. To validate these findings and provide practical guidance for wireless packet transmission, this research examines and presents numerical results for various scenarios, including outages, high-endurance communications, and time-fractional AoI. The Guderley problem is a traditional method for assessing the reliability of computer programs in hydrodynamic simulations, specifically those dealing with conic flows. Initially studied in the 1930s, the problem involves a weakly explosive axisymmetric flow of an incompressible fluid with a velocity gradient profile characteristic of all conic types. We examine the variability of these solutions in relation to different flow types and offer a framework to guide the evaluation of hydrodynamic simulations and codes through benchmarking against such fundamental reference solutions. We also compare our results with existing numerical studies, including those utilizing other methods such as the similarity method and shock hydrodynamics, to validate their accuracy.
