This paper introduces MrSARP, a hierarchical deep-generative model, which utilizes a complex structure of nested latent variables to synthesize detailed images at multiple resolutions through a single process. By merging multiple variants of the SRVAE model, MrSARP maintains SRVAE's ability to learn high-level artistic concepts while integrating them with low-level image features. We demonstrate MrSARP's effectiveness in exploring the latent space of an image, which allows the model to coherently generate images at multiple resolutions. Additionally, MrSARP can accurately estimate the conditional posterior of latent variables given observed images using a Monte-Carlo sampling approach. We evaluate MrSARP's performance on both generative and inference tasks, which include generating multiple resolution images, manipulating image attributes, and altering attribute combinations, as well as generating realistic images from scratch. Furthermore, MrSARP can perform various attribute manipulations with minimal adjustments to our model implementation. We also include an analysis of the hierarchical structure of MrSARP, which reveals the distinct contributions of different layers to the synthesis of images at different resolutions. Our experiments show that MrSARP outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches in generating detailed zonal maps, which are commonly employed in the game industry. Moreover, the generative model developed in this study is designed to be auto-conditioned, which enables the synthesis of multiple resolution images via a single latent variable. This approach can be applied to various visual tasks that demand coarse-to-fine resolution synthesis. All the model's source code and generated images are available on our website at https://sarp.corralservices.com. This study introduces a unified framework for actor-critic methods in the context of off-policy reinforcement learning. Within this framework, we identify and analyze various algorithms that compute the density function of the Gibbs measure using different approaches to integrating the q-function. The work expands upon prior research that relied on a specific relationship between the q-function and a distribution known as the uniform measure. By examining the differences in how each algorithm handles the breaking down of a large expectation into smaller components, we show that a first-order approximation of the gradient of the value function is achievable under mild conditions. The results are validated through both theoretical and empirical evidence. Empirically, the algorithms are found to be effective in handling challenging policy-recovery issues that arise from a partial action-space rollout. The evaluation is conducted on algorithms such as A2C, A2PW, SAPG, and COPG, which are observed to yield better performance than PPO, TRPO, and GO. The code is available at https://github.com/arghi/UnifiedFramework. One of the key advantages of the framework is its ability to support algorithms with reduced computational complexity. Lastly, the framework is found to support the computation of counterfactual policies through a general approach. Incidental posa spine fractures discovered by dual-energy X-ray transverse images require precise vertebra identification and localization for treatment planning. However, the low quality of images and limited information about vertebrae make this a complex task. We propose an integrated approach for posa spine fractures diagnosis and vertebrae identification and localization that leverages orientation-aware convolutional neural networks. By conducting experiments on 99 dual-energy X-ray transverse images, we achieved a 99% identification rate for vertebrae and a 98% accuracy rate for corresponding localization. Additionally, the results indicate a significant improvement in identification and localization times under image noise conditions compared to current benchmark methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method on a sample case and through a statistical analysis, which confirms the clinical relevance and robustness of the approach. The ability of piezoelectric materials to transmit energy via acoustic waves is linked to their properties at the material surface. Understanding the electroacoustic coupling at the boundary is essential in determining the "complete transmission" phenomenon when two materials couple. With the development of atomistic simulation techniques, it's now possible to investigate how atomic structures impact this energy transfer at the material interface. This study uses finite-terminations of infinite atomic chains in a density-functional perturbation theory framework to analyze transmission and reflection of longitudinal acoustic waves at piezoelectric surfaces. It's found that spontaneous polarization and spontaneous strain caused by finite atomic terminations lead to noticeable changes in reflection and transmission under both non-metallic and metallic surface conditions. However, these effects can be minimized by introducing a mirror image of the terminating atoms within the adjacent material. For piezoelectric semiconductors with a non-metallic surface, it's possible to achieve complete transmission by aligning the work function with the acoustic energy of the incoming wave using an appropriate detector bias. In contrast, piezoelectric metals require a specific surface electrostatic potential to achieve complete transmission. This study provides a theoretical foundation for controlling energy transmission between materials through their surface properties and also presents a novel method for detecting spontaneous polarization and spontaneous strain at material surfaces. Furthermore, the proposed complete transmission idea may lead to the development of highly efficient piezoelectric energy harvesters. Lastly, the study explores the possibility of manipulating piezoelectric nanostructures at the atomic level to tailor the energy transmission properties as desired. With the emerging nanotechnology advancements, it's now feasible to design and fabricate such nanostructures and thus pave the way for significant advancements in piezoelectric energy technology. The research has also been extended to include the simulation of actual piezoelectric samples with finite thickness, revealing that the energy transmission effect can lead to a considerable charge build-up upon application of an external mechanical stress, especially in nanostructured materials. This study provides a deeper understanding of the energy transmission phenomenon at the atomic level and demonstrates its potential to influence piezoelectric nanostructures and other materials with strong electroacoustic coupling. The research can also be applied in the development of various piezoelectric technology, including energy harvesting, sensing, actuation, and generation of voltage based on mechanical stimuli. We investigate a type of photon-polariton system that can be controlled through spatial light modulation, using excitation beams directed at a $\xi$-shaped microcavity filled with gain material and surrounded by an array of antenna-like structures. By adjusting the excitation beam's parameters and their interactions with the spatial light modulation, we are able to create complex patterns of polariton condensates that can persist for a significant amount of time. Our findings show that high-resolution spatial control of the excitation beams and the rapid modulation of their interactions can be used to fine-tune the condensates' properties and enable their rapid switching in response to varying external conditions. We explore the potential of implementing advanced optical techniques to refine the spatial and temporal focus of the excitation beams and examine the effects of introducing optical gain and non-local interactions on the condensates' behavior as well as their integration with advanced optical micro-devices. Throughout our investigation, we greatly simplified the complex dynamics of the system by employing a combined approach of theoretical and experimental analysis and the utilization of the non-equilibrium stationary state as a tool to understand the system's behavior. Our study showcases the remarkable potential of polariton condensates to be used in highly advanced optical micro-devices and presents a new frontier for the investigation of their integration with advanced optical technology. Moreover, we provide an in-depth analysis of the mode competition phenomenon in the system and examine the effects of varying the excitation beam's parameters on the condensates' behavior and their switchability in response to external conditioning. Our findings may find applications in the development of fast-switching optical systems as well as the creation of complex polariton patterns for the study of photonic characteristics. Lastly, we explore the possibility of using groundbreaking 3D optical technology to refine the focus and control of the excitation beams and evaluate its effects on the polariton condensates' behavior and switchability. This research may open up new avenues for the study of polariton condensates in highly advanced 3D optical settings.

Historians have long noted that Galileo's focus on observational methods lacked a clear connection to the underlying scientific principles.  As a result, his friends and colleagues in the Aristotelian school were able to effectively criticize his work.  In turn, this led Galileo's colleagues in the new scientific community to view him as an experimenter rather than a theoretical physicist.  Although Galileo's role in the scientific revolution is often seen as a transition from the medieval to the modern era, his unique position within this transition is worth exploring in more detail.  As a key figure in the scientific revolution, Galileo's contributions were instrumental in laying the foundation for the scientific method as we know it today.  Furthermore, his work had a significant impact on the development of various scientific fields, including physics, astronomy, and mathematics.  In this article, we will examine Galileo's contributions to the scientific revolution and explore how his unique perspective as a key figure in this transition enabled him to play a crucial role in shaping the scientific method itself.  By doing so, we will uncover the complexities of Galileo's role in the scientific revolution and how his ideas and actions were influenced by the social and cultural contexts in which he lived and worked.  Specifically, we will explore how the intellectual tensions between the Aristotelian and new scientific communities in 16th and 17th century Italy affected Galileo's thinking and how his relationships with other prominent figures in this period were marked by power struggles and competing interests.  In addition, we will examine how Galileo's role in the University of Padua and his connections to the Medici family and the Catholic Church influenced his access to resources and the social dynamics of the networks in which he was embedded.  By incorporating insights from the broader social and cultural contexts in which Galileo lived and worked, we will draw on the methods of and theories in the history of science to provide a more nuanced understanding of the social and cultural complexities of the scientific revolution and how they affected Galileo's contributions to the scientific method.  In this revised version of the article, we will provide a more detailed analysis of the intellectual tensions between the Aristotelian and new scientific communities in 16th and 17th century Italy and how these competing interests affected Galileo's relationships with other prominent figures in this period. We introduce a concept of binding q-energy to extend the principles of binding energy, a fundamental idea in non-Gaussian statistical mechanics. The binding q-energy reflects the total energy influence of interactions within a system according to a specific set of parameters, defined by q-chromatic number. This energy measure is compatible with standard binding energy under specific conditions (q=1) and shares similarities with other energy concepts like interaction coefficients and hyperinterpolation energy. The binding q-energy is a comprehensive mathematical quantity that encapsulates the inherent properties of statistical mechanics systems, offering a valuable tool for categorizing and analyzing such systems. Through a systematic study approach, we derive the properties of binding q-energy in detail. In order to ascertain whether Digital Assistants (DAs) can attain human-like
cognitive capabilities, we examined the development of a DA capable of
self-improvement through interactions with human collaborators in a problem-
solving task. The DA was trained by engaging in a series of joint problem-solving
activities with human partners, during which it learned to take on various roles
and generate plans to achieve shared goals. As time passed, the DA displayed
increasing proficiency in adapting its strategies, demonstrating intuition and
complex problem-solving abilities similar to those of human assistants. By
emphasizing the significance of collaborative learning and the emergence of
advanced capabilities from interactive processes, our findings offer a new vision
for the advancement of DA cognition. Moreover, our results highlight the value of
human-DAs interactions as a means of advancing both human and DA performance.
